#3060. How To Do Better Influencer Marketing

Agung Dwi Sandi is the Founder and CEO of rankpillar Group, an expert marketing and leading digital marketing agency in Southeast Asia.

Influencer marketing has stopped being an experiment. According to the World Federation of Advertisers’ 2025 research, 99% of member brands work with influencers, 66% do so frequently and global creator partnership spend is expected to pass $39 billion this year. The discipline has professionalized quickly on the compliance side: 70% of brands say they always sign contracts, and 66% have a written influencer policy.

What has not professionalized at the same rate is what brands actually ask for.

I run a digital marketing agency in Southeast Asia. Across the region, a large paid-amplification economy has grown up. In Indonesia, it is commonly called the buzzer industry: loosely organized networks of social accounts, assembled by coordinators, that will post on a brand’s behalf for a fee priced per account, per post, per day.

Comparable structures exist in most high-engagement social markets. Indonesia’s is simply unusually visible and unusually cheap. Enforcement is now almost entirely automated: KOL.ID’s read of transparency data puts TikTok’s proactive removal rate in Indonesia at 99.3%.

The briefing conversations I have with brands buying this kind of amplification follow one script. How many accounts can you mobilize? How many posts a day? Can we be trending by Friday? What almost never comes first is the only question that decides whether any of it works: What should a specific person believe or do differently after they see this?

That gap is structural rather than ethical. Read what this part of the market charges for, and you have read its self-definition: accounts, posts, days and impressions. Nothing on that price list is an outcome.

Buyers are not innocent either. In the same WFA research, reach (94%) and engagement (89%) dominate success measurement, while only 23% of brands use conversions or sales. Marketing Dive reported this month that about two-thirds of marketers surveyed by the Association of National Advertisers call measurement the hardest part of influencer work.

When a buyer cannot measure an outcome, they buy what they can count. Volume is countable, so volume becomes the product.

There are four key changes that I believe will separate brands that buy influence from brands that buy noise.

A brief is not a document; it is a set of decisions: Who are we talking to, what do they currently believe, what do we need them to believe instead, what are we asking them to do and what evidence would we accept to show that it worked?

Hand a vendor 200 posts to place, and you have given them a logistics problem. Logistics firms are good at logistics. What they cannot do is tell you that your positioning is the thing that is broken. If the first thing you receive back is a rate card, you were never buying marketing.

The WFA’s own recommendation is to look past follower counts and look toward audience alignment and genuine product affinity.

In our creator work, candidates pass three gates before price is discussed: whether their audience actually sits in the geography the client sells in, whether their recent short-form content earns real view-through rather than borrowed spikes and whether the content would survive being placed next to the brand’s own. We source candidates through application-based creator hubs, where creators opt in to a campaign rather than being bulk-booked by a coordinator, which makes consent and fit inputs to the brief instead of afterthoughts.

Matching is slower and far harder to sell than mobilizing a hundred accounts. It is also the only part of the process that compounds.

The ANA’s guidance is to set an end goal, whether it’s sales, conversion or awareness, before launch. Go one step further and define the disproof. A credible answer involves a holdout group, a before-and-after measure or, at minimum, a number agreed upon in writing that nobody can reinterpret afterward.

Ask a prospective partner what they would accept as evidence the campaign failed. The quality of that answer tells you more than any case study.

The ANA recommends assigning a single internal group to manage creator relationships, and the WFA finds marketing departments leading this work in 54% of organizations.

The question to settle internally is simple: Who writes the brief? “Send us the brief, and we will execute” is a supplier’s answer. That may be exactly what you need, but do not then expect the result to be a strategy. Ask a partner, too, what they would remove from your plan. A labor vendor will add scope because scope is revenue. A partner will subtract whatever does not serve the objective.

Generative tools have collapsed the marginal cost of producing and distributing content with streamlined drafting, variation, translation, scheduling and just sheer volume. A business whose value proposition is the supply of execution labor is being repriced in real time, and a brand whose strategy is the purchase of execution labor is buying an input its competitors can now acquire for almost nothing.

What does not commoditize is judgment about an audience, a point of view worth amplifying and the instrumentation to know whether either worked. In the campaign data I see, the distance between paid volume and genuine attention has widened over the past two years, which makes a warehouse of accounts a depreciating asset rather than an unfair advantage.

The amplification economy did not grow because marketers in my market are careless. It grew because it answers, cheaply and instantly, a question that is easy to ask: How much noise can I buy?

The harder question has no rate card: What is the one thing people need to understand, and how will we know they understood it? Write that down before you brief anybody. If a vendor cannot argue with your brief, they cannot improve your marketing. They can only make it louder.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This morning the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) dropped the October Consumer Price Index, which shows that inflation rose another 0.4% last month. This outpaced expectations: Economists had forecasted an increase of 0.3%. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, and futures traders are banking on a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Central bankers raised the federal funds rate in September, but it hasn’t been enough to pull inflation closer to the Fed’s target of 2%. Investors aren’t sure that one more hike in December will do the trick, either. According to CME FedWatch, further rate hikes may be in store for January.

#3057. Texas Wants to Rethink Data Center Construction. Here's the AI Stock Most Exposed.

Oracle's extensive presence in the Lone Star State puts it in the spotlight.

The recent push in Texas to pause data center construction has sparked concerns across the AI industry. This applies in particular to cloud companies, which have driven the rapid development of these facilities amid rising demand.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott had some state agencies audit data center requests beginning in August. In September, he ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt the issuance of final permits for data center projects. This moratorium effectively paused all new data center development until at least December.

The concerns that created these pauses aren't going away, and they were likely escalated after Gina Hinojosa's upset victory in the 2026 Texas gubernatorial election. The public sentiment around data centers is growing increasingly negative.

Most cloud companies have some business interests in Texas, but the most affected is likely to be Oracle (ORCL +8.81%). Fortunately, the current actions around data centers could create more of a buying opportunity than a risk to the stock.

The Oracle footprint in Texas is extensive.

The company chose areas around Abilene for its largest deployments, citing the region's capacity to generate wind and solar power. Moreover, it has placed capacity in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, as that is one of the world's most interconnected corridors for data centers. Furthermore, even though it plans to relocate its corporate headquarters from Austin to Nashville over the next few years, Austin remains its operational base for now and is a hub for hosting.

Fortunately, despite Oracle stock being on pace for its worst year since 2001, Oracle investors may not need to panic. For one, Hinojosa proposed a moratorium on new data centers, which does not apply to current facilities or those under construction. This gives the company the opportunity to build more outside of Texas if necessary.

Secondly, the moratorium would presumably remain in effect only until new regulations are in place. Hence, the change in leadership may only have minimal effects on Oracle's data center plans within the Lone Star State.

Oracle may also be in better financial shape than the many bears fear. Admittedly, the data center construction boom is the main factor in its more than $125 billion in total debt, a level well above the company's $67 billion book value.

Still, in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended Aug. 31), revenue of $19 billion increased by 30% from the same quarter last year. Most of that growth came from the cloud segment, which accounts for 60% of total revenue.

Nonetheless, the other 40% consists of its legacy businesses. Should the cloud segment struggle, these other enterprises could provide Oracle with stability. This gives Oracle stock an advantage over a company like CoreWeave, which is totally dependent on the cloud for its revenue.

Moreover, investors should note that Oracle's fiscal Q1 net income of nearly $4.8 billion rose 63% from the year-ago period. Since that figure also includes $1.4 billion in interest expenses, Oracle can presumably afford to service its loans.

Amid debt concerns, the cloud stock now trades near 52-week lows. However, its 20 P/E ratio is close to its lowest valuation since the pandemic. That could make the stock worth buying despite the risks of its Texas exposure.

Although Oracle has heavy exposure to Texas, it appears well-positioned to manage the state's political shift.

Hinojosa's proposed moratorium on data center construction would only apply to future projects, leaving Oracle's current Texas operations unaffected.

Additionally, Oracle benefits from rapid expansion, bolstered by well-established legacy businesses, providing both growth and stability. When considering its discounted stock price and ability to service its considerable debt load, Oracle investors probably do not need to worry about Texas's political shift.

#3056. Why The AI Race Is Also A Chemistry Race

Dr. Ahmed Ismail, founder of Dunia Innovations and Aquature, builds AI-driven autonomous labs and technologies for energy and chemicals.

​Here is a trivia question for your next board meeting: Which company holds a near-monopoly on a material that sits inside the package of almost every advanced AI chip? If you said Nvidia or TSMC, you are in good company, but you are wrong. It is Ajinomoto, the Japanese company best known for MSG.

Ajinomoto Build-up Film, or ABF, insulates the dense wiring in the substrate that an AI processor is fixed on. Since a leading CPU maker adopted it in 1999, ABF has reportedly captured more than 95% of its market. In 2026, riding the AI boom, the electronic-materials business built around it reported operating margins above 50%.

I love this story because it exposes a blind spot. We talk about AI as models and parameters, yet every GPU is a stack of chemistry, engineered atom by atom for over 70 years, and that chemistry is fast becoming the hardest part of the race.

In the 1980s, chip technology was based on about 12 chemical elements. By the 2000s, it used more than 60 elements. A 2025 preprint estimates that the industry now relies on over 85% of all non-radioactive elements.​

Some of AI’s material problems, like ABF supply, are about scale, and capital may fix them. The harder problems are physics walls, where the materials we need do not exist yet.

These physical walls include wires, heat and space.​

As chips shrink, copper wiring starts to behave like a resistor. Below roughly 17 by 17 nanometers, ruthenium’s resistivity drops below copper’s.

In 2024, Nvidia’s thermal engineers reportedly saw two-phase direct-to-chip cooling as the preferred route for next-generation accelerators. Its classic fluids, however, belong to the PFAS family of forever chemicals. 3M completed its exit from PFAS manufacturing at the end of 2025. Someone has to invent the replacement.

On October 1, 2026, Google launched a prototype satellite carrying four of its AI chips to test how they handle radiation and the thermal extremes of orbit. With no air or water to carry heat away, space behaves like an insulator, and heat can only leave by radiation. Without better coatings to radiate that heat, an orbital data center will be a materials problem first before it solves a computing problem.

Nvidia has committed to what Jensen Huang calls a “one-year rhythm” for new AI chips. A new material, by contrast, commonly needs 10 to 20 years to go from discovery to deployment. So we may soon see a big mismatch between an industry moving at software speed that is building on a foundation that moves at chemistry speed.

The good news? The same technology hungry for new materials is finally good enough to help find them. Better materials make better chips, better chips train better models and better models can search the chemical space faster than any human team. That loop makes the AI race and the chemistry race one and the same.

In November 2025, the U.S. launched the Genesis Mission, a Department of Energy effort to link national-lab supercomputers and datasets with autonomous, AI-directed experiments. In July 2026, the White House said more than $5 billion in federal commitments were being made to expand it. The AI labs are moving, too. In December 2025, Google DeepMind said that it would open a UK lab in 2026, where robots could make and test hundreds of materials a day.

Frontier models have already read much of the internet’s text and code. The next great dataset has to come from the lab, failed experiments included. Governments and AI labs are betting that the most valuable data comes from touching the physical world.

In 2023, Google DeepMind’s GNoME model predicted 2.2 million new crystal structures. When two materials chemists at UC Santa Barbara examined a sample in 2024, they found “scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility.”

I know this simulation-to-reality gap firsthand. During my graduate research at synchrotron facilities in France, Germany, the U.S. and Japan, I watched catalysts at work under X-ray beams, and these materials rarely stayed the same during the chemical reaction. Inside the reactor, they kept reshaping themselves until they settled into a final form that was different from the original one. How could a computer simulation have predicted this?

A computer can propose a thousand candidates, but only a furnace, a reactor or an X-ray beam can tell you which candidate is real. Building an autonomous lab taught my team the same lesson: The scarcest and most valuable resource is the capacity to make and measure candidates quickly, under realistic conditions.

What does this mean for technology leaders today? Start with a few first steps:​

• Map your AI roadmap down to its materials. For every plan, ask what it physically needs. If the answer is a material that does not exist yet, it goes on your risk register, right next to your supply chain risks.

• Treat experimental data as a strategic asset, failures included. The failed experiments in lab notebooks are useful data, too. In a 2016 Nature study, a model trained on a research group’s archived lab notebooks, including failed reactions, recommended experiments that worked 89% of the time. Experienced chemists got 78%.

• Judge AI claims by the physical proof in the lab. When someone announces a million new materials, ask how many were actually made and how many were stable under realistic conditions. One million predicted candidates is just a list of hypotheses. A novel material that survives weeks inside a real reactor is what we could call the start of a materials breakthrough.

The take-home message is simple: AI’s next big step depends on materials that don’t exist yet. The leaders who plan for that now will be the first to benefit when those materials arrive.​

Because the next move can’t be reliably predicted, the method doesn’t ask you to try. The calendar decides when you buy.

If prices rise, part of your money is already working. If they fall, your remaining thirds will likely buy cheaper and bring down the average you paid. Motley Fool co-founder David Gardner calls the approach “an incredibly effective win-win way to get invested in any volatile stock that’s trading high.”

We think buying in thirds is worth its small cost when two things are true. You believe the company will be worth meaningfully more three or more years from now. Without a plan, you’d keep waiting or put everything in at once on a hunch.

#3049. Car Insurance Soars for Drivers With Poor Credit; Here’s What to Do

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

While building your credit, shop around for auto insurance quotes. Some insurers are more lenient than others.

Lead Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

Your driving record may be spotless, but if you have poor credit, car insurance companies view you as a risk — and they’re significantly raising your rates.

Over the past three years, drivers with poor credit have seen auto insurance premiums surge 37.7%, according to NerdWallet’s 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report. These price hikes were even steeper than those faced by drivers with good credit who caused a crash or got a DUI.

In January 2023, someone with poor credit and a clean driving record would pay a median of $2,864 per year for full-coverage car insurance, NerdWallet’s analysis found. By January 2026, premiums for this driver had risen to $3,944 — an increase of $1,081 per year. By comparison, the same driver with good credit saw an increase of only $576.

“Credit scores are one of the most harmful things that results in you paying higher auto insurance premiums,” says Michael DeLong, a research and advocacy associate with the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “The penalties are extremely severe.”

While higher premiums after a wreck or DUI may not be a surprise, DeLong says many drivers aren’t aware their credit scores will affect their car insurance rates. To further complicate things, building credit can take months.

But there are ways to get relief more quickly. DeLong suggests comparing car insurance quotes from multiple companies, because some insurers penalize poor credit less than others. Raising your deductible, evaluating your coverage and avoiding small claims can also help.

NerdWallet’s analysis found that insurers raised rates more sharply from 2023 to 2026 for drivers with poor credit than for those with good credit — even if the poor-credit driver had a flawless record while the good-credit driver had a DUI, speeding ticket or at-fault crash.

When our sample driver with poor credit also had a recent DUI or speeding ticket, rate increases were even greater. Prices for a full-coverage policy went up by more than 40% for drivers with poor credit and a recent DUI, the biggest increase of any profile we analyzed.

Drivers often think it’s unfair for credit to affect car insurance prices, DeLong says, since it isn’t directly linked to driving behavior. Some states agree; California, Hawaii and Massachusetts don’t allow credit as a factor in setting auto insurance rates.

However, insurers say credit scores can indicate the likelihood that a driver will file a claim.[1]National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Credit-Based Insurance Scores. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources They use what’s called a credit-based insurance score — similar to the typical credit scores used by lenders but weighted differently.

“It helps in predicting expected claims activity and loss costs more accurately,” said Norman Niami, a member of the American Academy of Actuaries' Automobile Insurance Committee, in an email.

The practice has been controversial, with critics arguing it disproportionately hurts low-income and minority drivers. But a Federal Trade Commission report to Congress in July 2007 concluded that credit-based insurance scores were strong predictors of risk even when controlled for income, race and ethnicity.[2]A Report to Congress by the Federal Trade Commission. Credit-Based Insurance Scores: Impacts on Consumers of Automobile Insurance. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources

The explanation may be that some people simply tend to take risks, according to a statistical analysis published in the North American Actuarial Journal in 2016.[3]North American Actuarial Journal. Empirical Evidence on the Use of Credit Scoring for Predicting Insurance Losses with Psycho-social and Biochemical Explanations. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources Researchers concluded that risk-taking behavior can affect credit scores as well as insurance claims. Their analysis found that average losses per policy were 64.6% higher for drivers with the lowest credit scores than for those with the best credit.

Working to build your credit over time may help lower your car insurance premiums, but it’s not a sure thing. A credit-based insurance score is just one of many factors (along with things like location, age and driving history) that insurers use to rate a person’s risk.

Building credit “can produce a noticeable premium decrease in some cases, while producing little or no change in others,” Niami said, depending on whether the new score causes an insurer to move you into a better rating tier. Each insurer sets its own score thresholds, so a score viewed as “poor” by one insurer might be considered “fair” by another.

At the same time, consumer advocates argue it’s difficult for many people to take the steps needed to strengthen their credit scores.

“Most people probably have some idea that you can improve your credit score by trying to pay your bills regularly and reliably, and using different kinds of financial resources and credit cards,” DeLong says.

“But again, that’s easier said than done," he says. "If you’re struggling at a low-wage job and trying to juggle bills, or if you don’t easily have access to a credit card, that advice may not be especially helpful."

Drivers with poor credit or no credit may be able to take other steps to lower their premiums.

Comparing car insurance quotes from different companies is one of the best ways to ensure you have the cheapest rate possible. Insurers set their own pricing formulas, and some are more forgiving of poor credit than others. A NerdWallet analysis of October 2026 rates found that in about half (49.3%) of U.S. ZIP codes in states that allow credit scoring, the cheapest insurer for a driver with poor credit was a different company than the cheapest for a driver with good credit.

Although you can’t improve your risk profile overnight, “there’s a bunch of small things you can do that over a two- to three-year span make you look a lot better” to insurers, says Bradley Flowers, founder of Portal Insurance agency in Mobile, Alabama.

Consider a higher deductible. Raising your car insurance deductible — the amount of a future claim that you agree to cover yourself — lowers your premium and signals to insurers that you’re less likely to file a claim. But be sure you can afford to pay the higher deductible if you have to make a claim.

Adjust how you’re billed by insurers. By signing up for automatic payments and ensuring you don’t miss insurance payments each month, you’ll get a small discount while improving your risk profile for insurers.

Avoid minor claims if you can. Flowers recommends thinking twice about filing minor claims, such as windshield cracks. “When you’re in one of these situations, let’s save our insurance for the really bad stuff,” he suggests.

Lastly, be sure your coverage fits your vehicle. If you could afford to replace your car on your own, consider dropping collision and comprehensive coverage to bring your premiums down. Your trimmed-down policy would still provide you with liability coverage after a crash, while leaving you to cover damage to your vehicle.

NerdWallet's 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report is based on an analysis of more than 1.4 billion rate estimates provided by Quadrant Information Services for all 50 states and Washington, D.C., from January 2023 to January 2026.

Quadrant derives its rate data from modeled estimates based on carrier rating algorithms; figures do not reflect every available carrier or every consumer's individual rate. Liberty Mutual does not participate in Quadrant's rate data and is not represented in this analysis.

Quadrant’s figures are modeled rate estimates produced by running a fixed driver profile through carrier rating algorithms. They represent both new business and renewal rate estimates, and they are not a record of what actual drivers paid.

NerdWallet anchored its analysis to a 3-year old Toyota Camry LE, ensuring each analysis period reflected rates for the same-aged car.

The primary rate analysis is based on a 35-year-old single driver with good credit, no recent at-fault accidents or driving violations, and a full-coverage policy with $1,000 deductibles for collision and comprehensive coverage. Rates are pooled across male and female drivers.

In states where drivers must carry other types of insurance not included in our full coverage profile specifications, we added the minimum amount of coverage required by those states. Some policies include additional coverage at the insurer’s discretion.

In addition to our base profile driver with good credit and a spotless driving history, we analyzed rates for the following driver profiles:

Drivers with an at-fault crash. We added a single at-fault crash causing $10,000 in property damage.

Drivers with a speeding ticket. We added a single speeding ticket for driving 16 mph over the speed limit.

Drivers with a DUI. We added a single drunken-driving violation.

Drivers with poor credit. This is the same as our regular base profile, except the driver has poor credit instead of good credit. We also analyzed rates for drivers with poor credit and each of the three incidents above.

NerdWallet applied a strict comparability filter before calculating year-over-year figures. Only coverage variants and carrier/state combinations present in all four years of data were included in median calculations. This ensures reported changes reflect genuine pricing shifts among stable carriers, rather than differences caused by insurers entering markets, exiting, or going insolvent during the analysis period.

#3044. Why Fragmented Data Estates Can Drain Leaders' AI Budgets

“Context” is now the most overworked word in enterprise AI. Everyone uses it, but few mean the same thing. I use a narrow definition: Context is what an agent has to know before it can act. That means knowing what data exists, what it means, how it relates to everything else, when it’s valid and where to find it. That doesn’t come with the model. It must be built into the data estate, because an agent can’t ask the person who built the table.​

Skipping that work costs money. Without context, an agent will fall back on raw intelligence. It will search, guess and infer what it could have been told directly. You will pay in tokens for every wasted step, and each wasted step is another chance to get it wrong.​

Most enterprises aren’t there yet, which is why the bottleneck is in the data estate, not the model. In a 2026 survey Teradata commissioned from Wakefield Research, more than 75% of senior technology and data leaders estimated that 20% or less of their data is “ready for AI agents to use reliably.” Roughly the same percentage said they struggle to unify data and knowledge across business functions well enough for agents to reason across the enterprise.​

Those gaps don’t disappear when an agent gains access to the data; they become operational risks.​

Giving agents access to data without context to understand it is called context fragmentation: data that lacks the meaning, lineage and governance an agent needs to act reliably across an organization. Unlike humans, agents fail quietly. An analyst handed a revenue figure that looks wrong may stop and ask someone. An agent working from the same figure may act on it, and the mistake may surface weeks later.​

Organizations need to make sure their data carries enough meaning for agents to reliably utilize it. The more time an agent searches for an answer, the more time it has to hallucinate.​

If you’re relying solely on powerful models and prompt engineering to get the most out of your data, you’re doing it wrong.​

A brilliant model may not know which customer table finance trusts, but the same is true of a brilliant new hire. Point one at piles of paper and say, “Find me this answer.” They would have to read every pile before they could answer.​

Now put a Post-it note on top of each pile, describing what’s in them, what you won’t find, how the piles relate and which documents to pull first. The same person can find the right answer in a fraction of the time.​

Agents need the same notes. Without them, agents will explore every schema, guess at joins, run queries that fail or return the wrong thing, then try again.​

Context gets built in two layers. The bottom-up layer describes each source: what it holds, what it doesn’t, how it should be used and which other sources it joins to. That is one of a data product’s jobs: telling an agent what a dataset is before the first query.​

The top-down layer is an ontology. It defines the business: things it cares about, how they relate and what constraints they obey, regardless of which system holds the data. Neither layer works alone. Descriptions without an ontology give an agent well-labeled piles but no picture of how the business fits together. An ontology without descriptions has the opposite problem. It knows a customer should exist and how a customer relates to an order, but it doesn’t know where customer data lives, which data is correct for this use or whether anyone still maintains it.​

Take a simple question about last quarter’s revenue, for example. Ask sales, finance and billing, and you’ll receive three different numbers. Each team is right about its own number. The ontology says what revenue is and how it relates to customers and contracts. The descriptions say where each number lives and how current it is. Neither one tells the agent which number to use for the question in front of it.​

Building either layer by hand doesn’t scale. Both have to span every system the business runs, without moving the data first, because an agent’s question doesn’t stop at a platform boundary. Nobody is going to write notes for decades of tables. Much of the bottom layer can be discovered from the estate itself: what each source holds, where it came from, how it’s used and what it connects in practice. The top layer doesn’t have to start from a blank page either, because how a bank or a retailer works is already well understood broadly.​

But no amount of discovery or industry knowledge can supply what people in the business have never written down: which number counts and for which question.​

The returns from enterprise AI come when agents act on the business, not just answer questions about it. Governance is what lets you give them that authority. Someone must decide what an agent may do, what data it sees and on whose behalf, how long it runs, how much it spends and when a person has to sign off. Those limits can’t live in the prompt. A model can be talked out of an instruction, so the controls belong outside it, in the systems the agent acts through. And the enterprise should hold its own off switch rather than depend on a provider’s.​

Models can and should be interchangeable. Context and governance should stay with the enterprise when the model changes.​

The advantage is moving away from models, which everyone can rent, and moving toward giving each decision the context it needs and leaving out what it doesn’t. The advantage will go to the enterprises that put notes on the piles and agree on what the notes mean. Every definition they settle on is reasoning their agents no longer pay for, whichever model they run. Everyone else will keep paying the context tax.​

The innovation pipeline is robust under new CEO John Ternus.

The last few weeks have been difficult for technology investors. This is indicated by the 12% decline of the Vanguard Information Technology ETF since the start of October (as of Nov. 11).

Investors can blame the recent slide on Nvidia shares tanking. In addition to the chief executive officer's latest troubles, the market worries about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Even the smallest shift in sentiment can have a pronounced impact given how important these sorts of businesses are right now.

Amid the turmoil, Apple (AAPL +0.68%) looks like a winner. It's currently trading in record territory, with shares up 31% this year. The $5.2 trillion market capitalization easily makes it the world's most valuable company. It makes sense if investors view this as more of a consumer staples stock rather than a pure tech stock.

The business continues to operate as it always has, with fresh product releases a cornerstone of the strategy. The iPhone Duo and HomeView are the most notable launches. Will these innovations give Apple shares more room to run?

The stock's recent strength underscores its unique AI strategy. This business has not participated in the extraordinary infrastructure boom that's seeing its tech peers spend hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers, often raising external capital to do so. Capital outlays of this size naturally increase the financial risk investors must deal with.

And this puts the AI trade on fragile ground. The market wants rapid growth to continue for hyperscaler cloud platforms and the leading AI labs. No one can accurately predict what the industry will look like in two to three years, which is the problem that introduces immense uncertainty.

A premium brand defined by pricing power, customer loyalty, and an unmatched ecosystem make Apple an elite company. And the constant focus on innovation keeps consumers interested. But investors face a trade-off. In exchange for owning such a high-quality business, you give up the potential to capture outsize returns.

The valuation could be a headwind. Shares are at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 36.4, which doesn't present investors with a margin of safety. You essentially have to believe the market will continue to assign a high multiple to the stock.

Growth will also naturally slow. According to sell-side analyst estimates, Apple's revenue and earnings per share are expected to increase by just 27% and 31%, respectively, over the next three years.

This is accounting for the impact new products will have. The iPhone Duo immediately saw incredible demand. But the consensus view is that it will only represent 7% of iPhone revenue this fiscal year.

And it's too early to draw any conclusions about HomeView. However, this will have a tiny near-term financial impact even if tens of millions of units are sold.

These could end up being extremely successful products. The issue is that Apple is so massive, with fiscal 2026 net sales coming in at $479 billion. It's virtually impossible to move the financial needle at this size.

This isn't to say that the stock can't continue its ascent. It's just important that investors set the right expectations if they do choose to buy Apple.

#3039. $500 Invested in Boeing Today Could Be Worth This Much in 3 Years

Achieving production and certification milestones by 2029 could drive a 46% share price increase in the aerospace and defense giant's stock price.

If Boeing (BA -0.29%) hits a few milestones, the company could look much stronger in a few years, potentially driving a substantial rise in its share price. Here's what that could mean for investors dipping their toes into the market with a $500 investment in Boeing.

Management has set a medium-term target of $10 billion in free cash flow (FCF), and hitting it would show the company's returning to what might be called "normalized operations." In other words, it would mean ramping up production and deliveries of its narrow-body 737 MAX and its established wide-body 787, while certifying and making the first delivery of its new wide-body, the 777X.

Unfortunately, the company disappointed on that front recently by pushing back expectations for 737 MAX production, and the stock sold off accordingly. Still, I think there's reason to be optimistic based on Boeing management's new guidance.

CFO Jesus Malave outlined that the "building blocks of a $10 billion" in FCF "on a normalized basis" means a delivery rate of 52 a month on the 737 MAX, a delivery rate of 10 a month on the 787, and "a delivery rate and positive cash generation on a 777X program."

All those building blocks could fall into place and, in fact, be surpassed by 2029. First, management expects the 777X to receive certification, make its first delivery next year, and become cash-flow positive in 2029. Meanwhile, management expects to reach a production rate of 52 per month on the 737 MAX in the second half of 2027 and to transition to a production rate of 10 per month on the 787 this year.

While deliveries usually lag production by a few months, these operational targets suggest the "building blocks" of $10 billion in FCF could be in place by the end of 2027 -- implying Boeing could hit its FCF target earlier than in 2029.

As for valuation, $10 billion in FCF and a 20x price-to-FCF multiple imply a $200 billion market cap, or a 46% increase, meaning $500 invested now could be worth $730 in three years, with upside potential from a more aggressive ramp in 737 MAX production.

#3030. $1,000 Split Across These 3 Cybersecurity Stocks Could Be Worth This Much in 5 Years

AI is making hackers faster and more dangerous, but Fortinet, Cloudflare, and CrowdStrike have shown investors how they plan to win as the technology advances.

Here's a simple way to think about cybersecurity stocks right now: Companies are handing more of their work to artificial intelligence, and hackers are using AI more, too. That turns robust cybersecurity from a nice-to-have into the essential lock on the front door, and three companies in that industry just shared news that hints at where they'll be in five years.

Split an investment of $1,000 evenly across Fortinet (FTNT -2.10%), Cloudflare (NET -1.96%), and CrowdStrike (CRWD -4.31%), and you'd put about $333 into each. In my base cases for how those stocks will perform, that $1,000 would grow to roughly $1,500 by late 2031. These are my own scenarios, built on how fast I expect their sales to grow each year and what valuations investors will be willing to pay for them.

Fortinet sells firewalls -- the boxes that decide what gets into a company's network. On Oct. 28, it reported third-quarter revenue up 20% to $2.08 billion, with product sales, mostly hardware, up 37%.  But it trimmed its forecast for service revenue -- the subscriptions that customers continue to pay after they buy the boxes -- to a range of $5.15 billion to $5.17 billion, down from $5.18 billion to $5.22 billion three months earlier. The stock sold off hard and now trades around $122, down from a 52-week high near $197.

I think the market is reading that backward. CFO Christiane Ohlgart said big new customers switch on their subscriptions in stages, and pointed out that service billings, which offer an early look at future subscription revenue, grew by 26%. Management also expects service revenue to grow faster in 2027 than in 2026.

My five-year scenario: Fortinet sales will grow at an annualized rate of 12% a year, well below this year's pace, and investors will pay 20% less per dollar of sales than today. That would turn a $333 stake into one worth roughly $470.

Cloudflare runs a giant network in front of millions of websites, blocking attacks and speeding up traffic. On Nov. 5, it reported third-quarter revenue up 39% to $782.5 million, its fastest growth rate in nearly four years. It added more than 158,000 paying customers in the quarter, and developers building on its platform jumped from 7 million to 10 million in three months.

What I like most is how it wins them. CEO Matthew Prince said that when AI labs find new software flaws, they quietly tell Cloudflare, which protects customers "whether they pay us or not." He described small banks facing a "tsunami of threats" being pointed by peers and others to Cloudflare. The company also expects to deliver a GAAP profit this quarter, well ahead of its 2028 target.

The catch for investors is the stock's valuation. At about $294 a share, Cloudflare trades at around 32 times this year's expected sales. However, if sales grow 28% a year (slower than they have recently) and that P/s multiple gets cut in half, $333 will still become about $573.

CrowdStrike's Falcon software monitors laptops, servers, and logins for break-ins. Now it's also watching AI agents, programs that complete assigned tasks on their own. On Nov. 3, it agreed to buy Fiddler AI, which tracks what AI agents did and why, and CEO George Kurtz called Fiddler "the flight recorder for every agent."

Here's why that matters. When a plane goes down, investigators pull the black box. When an AI agent sends money to the wrong place, boards and regulators will want answers, and I'd bet the vendor that can produce them will win cybersecurity contracts. Annual recurring revenue, the yearly value of its subscriptions, grew 25% to $5.84 billion last quarter, and CrowdStrike raised its outlook for new subscription growth.

CrowdStrike is also the priciest of the three, trading at about 37 times this year's expected sales. If sales grow 22% a year and that multiple is cut in half, $333 will turn into about $450. That's my lowest scenario, not because the business is weakest, but because investors today have to pay the largest premium up front. If that worries you, building your stake in CrowdStrike by buying shares gradually over time is a reasonable way in.

In my scenarios, the $333 in Fortinet grows to about $470, Cloudflare's to about $573, and CrowdStrike's to about $450, so the original $1,000 would be worth roughly $1,500 in five years. That's not a guarantee, but if AI keeps making security a must-have, splitting your investment across these companies gives you portfolio exposure to a cheaper comeback story, a fast grower, and a leader in AI security.

#3028. Post-Quantum Cryptography Is No Longer The Future. Post-Cyber Is.

Distinguished Engineer at a global bank, ambassador for Microsoft & The Linux Foundation, transforming the future one giant step at a time.

​The biggest mistake we can make about quantum security is to think the problem is quantum.

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is no longer a research curiosity. In the fall of 2024, NIST finalized its first three (later more) post-quantum cryptographic standards, with a migration roadmap targeting the removal of quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography from its standards by 2035. The message is clear: Start migrating now. But I believe we are missing a larger conversation.

Quantum-safe cryptography addresses a specific mathematical vulnerability. It does not make our systems resilient. And resilience, not encryption alone, will define the next era of digital trust.

In the Snowflake customer breaches, attackers weren’t breaking encryption. They were logging in using stolen credentials. Mandiant identified approximately 165 potentially exposed organizations, with compromised accounts lacking multifactor authentication.

Then came the CrowdStrike outage. A faulty software update disrupted approximately 8.5 million Windows devices worldwide. Airports, financial services and critical infrastructure experienced disruptions.

Neither incident required a quantum computer. One involved compromised identities. The other involved a failure in trusted software. Both exposed an uncomfortable truth: We can have perfectly secure cryptography and still have catastrophically fragile systems.

Meanwhile, AI is making the situation more complicated. Threat intelligence from Google in 2026 documented increasingly sophisticated uses of AI in vulnerability research, exploitation and social engineering.

The attack surface is expanding faster than our traditional security boundaries.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could compromise RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, undermining much of today’s digital infrastructure. Nobody knows when that computer will arrive. In 2025, Google’s Craig Gidney published research suggesting RSA-2048 could theoretically be factored with fewer than one million noisy physical qubits under specific engineering assumptions, a dramatic reduction from previous estimates. And now we are down to a mere 10,000. This was not a prediction of imminent quantum capability. But it demonstrated how quickly assumptions can change.

And cryptographic migration takes years, sometimes decades. The “harvest now, decrypt later” threat makes waiting especially dangerous. Sensitive information intercepted today may become readable tomorrow. We absolutely need PQC.

But replacing one cryptographic algorithm with another cannot be our entire strategy.

History provides an important warning. The SIKE post-quantum candidate was undermined by classical cryptanalysis in 2022. The lesson wasn’t that post-quantum cryptography had failed. It was that we must design systems capable of changing their cryptography when assumptions fail.

Crypto agility matters as much as cryptographic strength.

When I say post-cyber, I don’t mean cybersecurity is disappearing. I mean cybersecurity as an isolated technical discipline is no longer sufficient. Through my work across enterprise technology, regulators and open-source communities, I’ve increasingly seen the difference between securing individual components and engineering trustworthy systems.

The former focuses on controls. The latter asks whether the business can survive when those controls, or the components they protect, fail. A post-cyber operating model connects six essential properties:

These aren’t new concepts. NIST CSF 2.0, zero-trust architecture, cyber-resilience engineering and CISA’s Secure by Design principles already address much of this territory. The missing piece is often organizational. We continue treating cryptographic migration, identity management, AI governance, software supply chains and operational resilience as separate initiatives. Attackers and failures don’t respect those boundaries. Neither should our architectures.

Apple’s PQ3 protocol for iMessage demonstrates an important architectural principle. Rather than simply replacing classical encryption, Apple adopted hybrid cryptography, periodic rekeying and mechanisms designed to recover from certain key compromises.

That’s the mindset we need beyond cryptography. Software updates should be staged and reversible. Dependencies should be visible. Identities should be continuously verified. Recovery should be engineered and tested, not assumed.

The first identifies cryptographic exposure: RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography, certificates, VPNs, applications, hardware and third-party dependencies requiring PQC migration. The second identifies systemic fragility.

What happens if privileged credentials are stolen? If a trusted supplier distributes defective software? If an AI agent operates beyond its intended authority? If a critical cloud dependency disappears? Knowing where vulnerable cryptography exists is essential. Knowing what can stop your business even when cryptography works perfectly is equally important.

Tracking the percentage of systems migrated to PQC is useful but insufficient. Leaders should also ask:

These questions turn security from a compliance exercise into a strategic capability.

Some will argue that post-cyber is simply another label for existing cybersecurity and resilience practices. That’s fair criticism.

We don’t need another acronym, compliance framework or organizational silo. What we need is a different way of connecting the disciplines we already have. PQC is one of the most consequential infrastructure migrations of this decade. It deserves urgent investment and serious engineering attention. But it cannot become another exercise in checking boxes while ignoring systemic weaknesses.

PQC asks whether our mathematics can survive a new kind of computer. Post-cyber asks whether our institutions, architectures and critical services can survive a world in which the assumptions beneath digital trust keep changing.

The first question now has standards, algorithms and a migration calendar.

#3026. Could $5,000 Invested in Nvidia Today Make You a Millionaire?

The scandal-rocked AI bellwether has a long way to go to become a 200-bagger from here. It can still crush the market.

Sometimes opportunity knocks. Other times, it just knocks you out. Nvidia (NVDA -13.63%) shed its market cap crown two weeks ago, and the gap continues to widen. The leading maker of AI chips and other high-level computing solutions has shed nearly 30% of its value since peaking last month.

The stock is surprisingly cheap right now. With a critical earnings report now less than a week away, is this a good place for your next investment? Delivering on the headline that brought you here, can laying $5,000 on Nvidia now make you a millionaire?

You probably know the answer. I have some hard truths if you don't.

Turning any $5,000 investment into a cool million will require patience. Nvidia stock would have to become a 200-bagger to hit seven figures. Put differently, Nvidia commands a market cap just above $4 trillion. There is only one other company on the planet with a higher price tag. Nvidia would have to top $800 trillion for a 200-bagger, and that is if Nvidia's share count doesn't increase over that time.

There is some good news on that front. Nvidia's been an aggressive buyer of its shares. It's been retiring more shares than it's been issuing for stock-based compensation or acquisitions. Its fully diluted share count is declining for the fifth consecutive fiscal year, a nearly 4% reduction over that time.

Nvidia is just getting started. Its board of directors recently announced a corporate record $150 billion in repurchase authorizations, boosting its buyback authorization to $235 billion. If Nvidia were to buy back $235 billion of its shares at current prices, it would reduce its share count by more than 5%.

Nvidia is making a lot of money. Next week we might find out that Nvidia is making even more money. It wouldn't be a surprise. It's been fairly consistent in delivering "beat and raise" performances, even if the shares initially move lower on the strong financials.

You're here for the long haul if you're expecting a 200-bagger to turn $5,000 into $1,000,000. The stock is cheap enough to beat the market for here. Nvidia is trading for less than 11 times next year's earnings estimates, as back-to-back scandals weigh on CEO Jensen Huang. It's going to be an interesting earnings call on Nov. 17, that's for sure.

Even bears have to agree that a company growing its business at a 90% clip -- the way its guidance calls for revenue and earnings growth in its upcoming fiscal third quarter -- is a compelling value. Growth will slow. Nvidia's chunky margins will contract. It's still a good price for what has historically been a great company.

So, can Nvidia really turn $5,000 into a million bucks? It's not a realistic expectation unless you have a decades-long investment horizon. However, it's a great start at an opportunistic time. Investing $5,000 today and continuing to add to that position over time can get you there. It's not the answer you wanted, but it's the response you needed to hear.

#3024. 16 Space-Based Technologies That Could Solve Business Problems

Advances in satellite technology, connectivity and data analysis are creating new ways for businesses to address challenges here on Earth. From monitoring infrastructure and tracking environmental risks to improving communications in remote locations, space-based capabilities are becoming increasingly practical across industries.

For businesses, the challenge isn’t simply gaining access to these tools—it’s identifying where they can improve decisions, boost efficiency and strengthen resilience. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council highlight space-based capabilities that are becoming practical for business use and explain the problems they could help solve.

Satellite radar can detect subtle ground movement around railways, pipelines and industrial sites, giving businesses early warning of infrastructure risks across vast networks. Paired with ground inspections, it helps operators target maintenance before damage escalates. The payoff: fewer costly shutdowns, smarter use of maintenance budgets, and better protection for people, assets and revenue. Its real value is turning unseen risks into actionable priorities. - Shelli Brunswick, SB Global LLC

Space-based weather and climate intelligence is becoming practical enough to shape operational decisions across industries. Hyper-local forecasts, severe weather tracking and climate risk modeling now draw on satellite data at resolutions that support utility grid planning, agriculture, insurance underwriting, logistics routing and renewable energy forecasting, leading to meaningful business and financial impact. - Nitin Agarwal, Luminace

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Satellite-based methane detection is becoming a practical business capability. Advanced orbital sensors can identify emissions at individual industrial facilities, enabling companies to detect costly leaks without extensive ground inspections. Integrating this intelligence with enterprise analytics transforms environmental monitoring into actionable insights that reduce operational losses and strengthen regulatory compliance. - Gouri Sankar Dash, Tata Consultancy Services

On-orbit AI processing is becoming practical enough to change how businesses use satellite data. Instead of sending massive amounts of raw imagery to Earth for analysis, satellites can process data in orbit and transmit relevant insights. That can reduce latency and bandwidth while enabling faster responses to disasters, infrastructure issues and other events. - Karan Alang, Versa Networks Inc.

Satellite-based Earth observation is becoming a powerful business tool these days. Using frequent imagery and AI analytics, companies can monitor crop health, detect supply-chain disruptions, assess natural-disaster damage and evaluate infrastructure risks. What once required costly, time-consuming field inspections can increasingly be done remotely, helping businesses make faster, data-driven decisions and build resilience. - Deepali Kaushik, NBCUniversal

Satellite-based flood monitoring can help companies protect construction sites and supply routes. Combine updated imagery with site and road data to identify exposure and prioritize inspections or rerouting. The value comes from turning that information into an operational decision, with people on the ground confirming conditions. - Shahen Minasyan, Twin Peaks Inc. (TPI)

Satellite-based maritime connectivity is finally becoming practical enough to keep ships connected far from shore. Having worked aboard cruise ships, I know how quickly isolation complicates operations. Reliable links can support live equipment diagnostics and faster medical consultations. Start with one critical shipboard system. Space technology earns its keep when it solves problems at sea. - Joel Frenette, TravelFun.ai

Space-based data centers are an exciting emerging capability. Companies like TakeMe2Space are exploring how computing infrastructure in orbit could address some of Earth’s data center challenges. While technical and economic hurdles remain, this approach could create new possibilities for processing data in space and reducing dependence on resource-intensive ground infrastructure. - Prashanthi Kolluru, KloudPortal Technology Solutions Pvt Ltd.

There’s satellite-verified proof of origin for supply chains. New rules on deforestation and forced labor require companies to prove where raw materials such as cocoa, palm oil or timber came from, down to the plot. Linking satellite imagery of those plots to supplier records and purchase orders in the ERP turns a paper declaration into evidence an auditor or customs officer can check. - Hari Sonnenahalli, NTT Data Business Solutions

Satellite broadband is now practical. It gives remote sites like mines, ships, farms and disaster zones low-latency links to the cloud where fiber can’t reach. Those edge locations can stream Internet of Things data, run cloud-based analytics, and stay online when local networks fail, so remote operations become connected and data-driven. - Srinivas Chippagiri, Salesforce Inc.

High-precision satellite positioning is becoming practical for construction, agriculture and autonomous operations. With real-time correction services, centimeter-level positioning can help businesses coordinate equipment, automate physical work and reduce costly errors. Location is becoming an operational signal, not just a point on a map. - Vibhor Kumar, EDB Postgres AI

Direct satellite connection to ordinary phones—which allows workers to stay reachable outside cell coverage—used to mean buying satellite hardware and training people to carry it, so most crews didn’t leverage it. Now a standard phone can send a message through a satellite from a dead zone. For the utilities, logging, mining and construction industries, that means a lone worker in a canyon can reach someone, and a supervisor always knows where the crew is. - Kriti Faujdar, Yelp

There’s satellite-based asset tracking for remote operations. Low-orbit connectivity now makes it affordable to monitor equipment, shipments and field crews in places cellular networks never reached. For businesses with assets at job sites, rail lines or rural facilities, that turns blind spots into live data on location, condition and usage, which means fewer lost assets and faster response. - Steven Singer, Arbill

Satellite monitoring of construction progress can help lenders decide when to release project funds. Imagery can verify whether a road, plant or housing phase has advanced as reported, flag stalled work, and direct inspectors to locations that need a closer look. That gives credit teams a cross-check between site visits, reducing delays in drawdowns without treating pixels as proof of workmanship. Each alert can be tied to human inspection and a documented payment decision. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

Low-Earth-orbit satellite internet’s lower latency and falling costs now support video visits, remote monitoring and image transfer in rural clinics that fiber never reached. Hospitals are also adding it as backup connectivity when storms or cable cuts take down terrestrial lines. For health systems, it closes access gaps and keeps clinical systems reachable during disasters. - Will Conaway, Tuxedo Cat Consulting

Satellite monitoring of harmful algal blooms is becoming practical for aquaculture and water-dependent businesses. Ocean color sensors can identify changes in water conditions that may indicate developing blooms. Fish farms and coastal operators can use these alerts to prioritize water testing and take protective action when needed. This helps reduce unexpected losses and supports better management of marine operations. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited

#3022. If You Buy and Hold Just 3 ETFs, History Says This Combination Is Your Best Bet

Two of these ETFs probably won't be surprising. The third one might be.

When most people think about investing in stocks right now, they think of the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.31%) and tech stocks. These groups have driven stock market returns for several years, and most people's portfolios are probably heavily concentrated in them right now.

But that doesn't always work out over the course of decades.

In the 2000-2009 decade, a pair of generational bear markets resulted in a lost decade for the S&P 500, where it lost 9% over that 10-year period. But some areas of the market didn't perform nearly as poorly. Financials and tech were clearly the biggest losers, but energy, consumer staples, small-caps, and emerging markets all posted strong returns.

It may not seem like it lately, but diversification still pays off. Investing in multiple areas of the market at once may not maximize your return potential at all times, but it'll probably smooth out the ride and limit some downside risk along the way.

You don't need a dozen ETFs to achieve diversification, either. In fact, you can hit almost everything you need with just a few of them. But if you're going to own just three ETFs to create a full portfolio, you have to make sure these funds are broadly diversified, cheap, and work well together.

Looking back over several decades of history, here's a three-ETF portfolio that might be your best bet as a long-term holding.

Any time I talk about portfolio construction, I usually start with the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.27%) as my core position. A lot of people will understandably use the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.73%) for this purpose. But I prefer VTI's inclusion of mid-caps and small-caps to cover the entire U.S. equity market.

The potential issue with this fund, of course, is its heavy concentration in tech stocks, which currently account for around 43% of the portfolio. That's clearly on the high side and exposes investors to some extra downside risk right now. If you want an alternative, consider the iShares MSCI USA Equal Weighted ETF (EUSA -0.25%), which has allocations of between 12% and 18% in four different sectors for better diversification.

International equity investing hasn't been popular for some time. U.S. stocks have outperformed them by a large margin, and the extra risk that comes from less developed markets just hasn't been paying off. That doesn't mean that international investing should be written off.

If you go back to the start of the 1970s, you'll see that U.S. and international leadership has rotated in multi-year cycles. Much of the 1970s and 1980s belonged to international. U.S. stocks outperformed in the 1990s, and international recaptured leadership in the 2000s. Since 2010, U.S. stocks have led in almost uninterrupted fashion.

The point is that international stocks are overdue for an extended stretch of outperformance, and they have a long history of doing that from time to time. The Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (VXUS +0.94%) is my pick for this. It invests in nearly 9,000 stocks across both developed and emerging markets, so you're capturing exposure to everything.

I'm guessing that the Vanguard Small-Cap Value ETF (VBR +0.06%) won't be a popular pick, given how poorly this segment has performed in recent years. But small-caps demonstrated how relatively well they can do in severely adverse markets from 2000-2009. That won't always be the case, but its potential for diversification and above-average long-term returns makes it worth considering.

This ETF is the way I'd play it. The undervalued nature of the portfolio helps limit some downside risk, and the sector composition offers a nice complement to what you'd get from the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF. Quality is usually an issue in the small-cap value category, but this portfolio is forecasted to deliver double-digit earnings and free cash flow growth, a good sign that fundamentals are in decent shape.

Together, these three ETFs should be able to deliver in multiple environments moving forward. They pair together well and should be able to provide a smoother ride in particularly volatile periods.

#3018. What Makes A VC Say Yes To A Founder

Mary Minno is a Founding Partner at Treehub.

Over the past year, I’ve backed 43 startups. This fall, I’m teaching Stanford School of Medicine’s AI Lab master’s course, training medtech entrepreneurs. Between investing at Treehub and teaching at Stanford, I spend my time thinking about what makes a founder successful. At Treehub, we’ve interacted with more than 700 startups over the past year—from polished pitches to brilliant scientists who have never pitched before and founders who can sell a vision but haven’t figured out how to build it.

There’s no one playbook to raise venture capital. Every investor has a different thesis and definition of potential. But reflecting on my time on both sides of the table, four qualities stand out to me.

And they aren’t necessarily what you’d expect.

The best founders can move between the big picture and the smallest details, explain how their company will transform an industry and then walk me through a technical challenge or what they learned from a failed experiment.

Vision without execution is just an idea. Execution without vision can lead to building something that never becomes a meaningful business.

This is particularly important in healthcare and AI. Scientists, physicians and researchers often understand a problem more deeply than anyone else. But building a company requires connecting that expertise to a bigger picture. Who needs this? Why now? How will it reach them? And how big could it become?

I don’t expect founders to know everything. I look for people who can connect what they know to what they still need to learn.

The best founders have an intangible quality that makes you want to keep listening. They paint a picture of what the world can become. They communicate in a simple, poetic way that captivates listeners, often with infectious energy.

It isn’t about being the loudest person in the room or having the slickest presentation. It’s about having contagious conviction that draws people in.

Building a company means convincing employees to join, convincing customers to try an unproven product and convincing investors to back a future you can’t guarantee. That takes the ability to communicate why an idea matters.

This storytelling is a skill founders can develop. What can’t be manufactured is genuine conviction. The best founders have an unmistakable connection to the problem they’re solving. They don’t just want you to understand their idea; they need you to understand why it matters.

Every founder has a vision. What separates those who build companies from those who don’t is how they respond when that vision collides with reality.

When a customer says no, a technical breakthrough takes longer than expected or a business model fails in practice, I want to know whether a founder can get creative, find another path and adapt without losing sight of the underlying problem.

Grit isn’t stubbornly pursuing the same strategy regardless of the evidence. It’s refusing to abandon an important problem just because the first solution didn’t work.

In my work, I often meet founders before they’ve created a pitch deck. Without revenue or customer traction to evaluate, I look at what they’ve already done with limited resources. Have they investigated the problem, challenged their assumptions and found ways to make progress?

Those actions reveal how they might navigate uncertainty when the stakes get higher. Resourcefulness before a company exists can be just as telling as traction after launch.

Building a company takes extraordinary time, attention and emotional energy. I don’t mean founders should sacrifice their health or relationships. Burnout isn’t a business strategy.

But there’s a difference between liking an idea and feeling compelled to solve a problem. Investors want to see the commitment to push through difficult stretches after the excitement of starting something new wears off.

This is especially relevant for scientists and clinicians. Turning years of research or firsthand experience into a business requires taking on challenges beyond your original expertise. Why this problem? Why are you the person to solve it? What have you seen that others haven’t? And why spend the next several years figuring it out?

A genuine connection between the founder and the problem can keep them moving when progress is slow and the path forward is unclear.

One of the biggest mistakes investors can make is confusing a founder’s ability to pitch with their ability to build.

Traditional venture capital relies on signals like revenue, growth and customer adoption. Those metrics matter, but they can cause investors to overlook people earlier in their journey. Waiting for them can mean overlooking exceptional founders before they’ve had the opportunity to prove themselves.

Some of the most consequential healthcare companies may come from researchers developing scientific breakthroughs, physicians who’ve witnessed persistent failures in patient care or technical founders who recognize opportunities others haven’t yet. They may not have a perfect pitch or an established network. That doesn’t mean they lack potential.

Of course, charisma, grit, vision and commitment don’t guarantee success. A founder still needs a real market, a viable business model and a solution that works.

But when I think about what makes me say yes, I return to four questions: Can this person connect the details to the vision? Can they bring others along? Can they navigate obstacles? And are they deeply committed to solving the problem?

Sometimes, the founder worth betting on isn’t the one who already knows how to build a company. It’s the one who has found a problem worth solving and can learn everything else along the way. As investors, our job is to recognize that potential before everyone else does.​​​

#3015. Wall Street's Next Blockbuster Stock Split Could Come From This Chip Equipment Giant

ASML posted record sales in its latest quarter, and some customers are already eyeing orders for delivery in 2029.

ASML Holding (ASML +1.76%) has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, thanks to its role in advanced chipmaking. In its third-quarter earnings announcement on Oct. 14, ASML reported record quarterly sales, with management citing continued strength in AI investments and customer equipment demand. With AI fueling another wave of demand for its equipment, the company's rising stock price could position it to conduct Wall Street's next major stock split.

ASML holds one of the most important positions in the AI supply chain. It's the world's only commercial supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which are necessary to manufacture all of the most advanced semiconductors.

Its customers include chip industry heavyweights like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Samsung, and Intel.

On top of that, ASML isn't a stranger to stock splits. It completed three during its earlier years: a 2-for-1 split in 1997, another 2-for-1 split in 1998, and a 3-for-1 split in 2000.

But it's been a while since ASML's last split, suggesting another one could be long overdue as its growth accelerates and pushes its share price higher.

When it comes to growth, ASML's management said that its current supply plans for 2027 and 2028 would not be sufficient to meet expected customer demand. In light of that, some customers are already expressing interest in placing orders for equipment deliveries as far out as 2029 and 2030.

And that brings us to another potentially important growth driver: ASML's newest generation of extreme ultraviolet lithography technology.

ASML's existing EUV technology is already nearly impossible for competitors to replicate -- if rivals do, it won't happen for years. However, the company isn't standing still. Specifically, it has developed High Numerical Aperture (High NA) EUV lithography equipment, which can print even smaller transistors and features, and thus fabricate more component-dense and powerful chips.

And one of the most encouraging developments is that High NA EUV technology is moving beyond experimentation.

For example, early adopter Intel has already processed more than 1 million wafers using the technology across equipment qualification, research and development (R&D), and production applications.

Meanwhile, other manufacturers are moving toward adoption.

For instance, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have outlined plans to introduce High NA EUV technology into their memory production beginning in 2028, while TSMC, the world's largest third-party chip foundry by far, intends to use it in high-volume manufacturing of advanced chips starting in 2030.

That matters because the future of ASML's next-generation technology doesn't depend on a single customer or application. Some of the world's biggest semiconductor manufacturers are already preparing to integrate it into their long-term production plans.

But despite its competitive advantages and technological monopoly, ASML still faces risks. For one, the chipmaking industry it supports is cyclical. If AI spending slows, chipmakers could delay their foundry expansion plans, potentially reducing demand for expensive EUV lithography equipment.

Plus, geopolitical restrictions and export controls, especially those that currently block the sales of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to customers in China, are ongoing headwinds to its sales growth. In addition, the company's reliance on highly specialized supply chains complicates production of its machines.

Regardless, given ASML's dominant position in chipmaking technology and the AI boom providing a strong growth catalyst, there are plenty of reasons why its stock belongs on retail investors' radars.

Analysts on Wall Street remain optimistic about ASML stock. In fact, the vast majority of analysts covering it rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average 12-month price target of over $2,100.

Meanwhile, the stock trades at around $1,550 per share and at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 23, which looks like a reasonable valuation, especially considering its competitive moat and long-term AI growth opportunities. That could leave room for further upside if earnings growth beats expectations.

Overall, ASML has a lot going for it, from its role in advanced chipmaking to the growing demand for AI infrastructure. If its growth continues to accelerate and pushes the stock higher, its first stock split in decades could be on the table, too.
