#3013. The Hidden Risks In Wealth Platform Migrations

Sharat Priya is a Senior Manager in EY’s U.S. Wealth & Asset Management Technology practice, leading wealth platform modernization.

The best migration is the one your clients never notice. Clients should see the benefits, not the disruption.

​Wealth platform migrations rarely fail on conversion weekend. The cutover finishes, reports turn green and problems appear later once real activity begins. A tax lot shows the wrong cost basis. A sweep runs an hour late. An outside manager calls to ask why a trade file never arrived.

In my 22 years in wealth technology, I’ve found that the most serious migration risks are often the least visible. They’re easy to miss during testing and only show up once the platform is live. Knowing where to look makes the difference.

Copying records from one database to another is the easy part. The real work is transforming them so they behave accurately under the new platform’s business logic. That takes business transformation rules, and a business owner must sign off on each of these mapping/transformation rules.

Critical data includes client and account records, relationships, standing instructions, transactions, cash balances, positions and tax lots. Even a single tax lot migrated incorrectly can change a client’s realized gain or loss—and with it, their tax obligation.

Complex instruments should be looked at more carefully. For mortgage- and asset-backed securities, check original face, current face and paydown factors. For Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), confirm the index ratio and inflation-adjusted principal. For pooled funds, verify units and unit values. Then run accretion, amortization, inflation adjustments, interest and paydowns through a full cycle and compare against the old system. These errors don’t appear on day one. They appear on the first factor date.

Every legacy platform holds years of settings: firm and region structures, users and entitlements, fee rules and schedules, ACH and wire cutoffs, sweep run times, corporate action recipients and approval thresholds. Most of it lives in the system, and very little of it is documented anywhere.

An inventory of such configurations should be prepared and compared line by line. Then decide what carries over, what changes and what goes away. Get entitlements wrong, and users can see client data they shouldn’t, which is a regulatory problem. Miss one approval step, and a large transaction executes without sign-off.

Before cutover, map each function on the old platform to its place on the new one. Some map directly. Some need a workaround. Some get retired. The gaps that cause problems are usually small, such as a custom fee discount or a report operation run every month.

New capabilities need the same attention: data, configuration and testing before they’re switched on.

A new platform changes who does what. For example, in one of the implementations I’ve seen, back-office operations moved to the platform provider. That shift needs a close look at what the firm still owns and which teams, roles, features, reports and controls change hands.

Then map current and future ownership; a RACI matrix helps. When no one owns the exception queue, unresolved items pile up, and clients are often the first to notice.

Vendor manuals and job aids explain the platform, not the use cases and custom scenarios specific to your firm. They should be tailored to the firm and built for the new operating model.

Timing can vary, but they must be ready before go-live so that staff know the new process on day one.

Controls don’t migrate automatically. Each existing control needs to be reviewed and set up again on the new platform.

Inventory current controls, including those covered in SOC reports. Decide which ones to retain, which ones to retire and which ones the new platform handles differently. Then enable any new ones it offers. Engage risk, compliance and internal audit early.

Advisors use client statements and performance reports. Operations uses exception reports. Finance uses billing reports, and compliance uses regulatory reports.

List the reports each team uses currently, and check how the new platform will produce each one: built-in, from a data warehouse or not at all. Run important reports on both platforms until the numbers match. Client statements must be right from day one.​

Integrations don’t carry equal risk. I sort them into three groups.

Core integrations, such as CRM, financial planning and trading systems, shape the advisor’s working day. External manager integrations matter wherever a third-party manager holds investment authority. Models, trade files and position feeds must keep flowing, and many of these relationships are shared with the firm’s clients, so a broken feed quickly becomes a client conversation.

Market data is the third group. Know which vendors will supply pricing, reference and corporate action data, and whether those feeds come ready-made or need new build and licensing work.

For each integration, know the owner, the testing window and the client sensitivity. Engage third parties early; they have their own release schedules.

Sometimes, a firm changes its custodian, clearing broker or cash agent during a platform migration. Find this out early.

In such cases, the firm may need to plan for client communication, updated account agreements and new reconciliation processes. These scenarios may also need additional steps during the conversion event.

Reconciliation is how the firm confirms that its records match those of its custodians and cash agents. It needs to work from day one.

Decide what will be reconciled (positions, transactions and cash), how often and what differences are acceptable. Decide who owns it: internal operations, the platform vendor or an outsourced provider. Set clear rules and tolerances for how long a mismatch can stay open before it is escalated.​

A migration isn’t just a technology project. It changes how the firm operates. Firms that get it right give each area a clear owner and test through full processing cycles so that the platform is accurate and meets the firm’s objectives before the go-live decision is made.

The best migration is the one your clients never notice. Clients should see the benefits, not the disruption.

#3009. Chevron's Production Fell. Its Profit Nearly Tripled. Here's How.

Fewer barrels, bigger profits: Chevron's latest quarter highlights the strength of its integrated business model.

Since the start of the year, the conflict in Iran has resulted in disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 million barrels of oil pass daily. Oil prices have jumped. More importantly, diesel fuel and other refined products have surged.

Chevron's (CVX +0.58%) third-quarter adjusted profit nearly tripled year over year to $10.4 billion, despite production declining 2.6%. The seemingly contradictory move illustrates the advantages of Chevron's integrated business model. Here's what investors should know.

As an integrated oil and gas company, Chevron's business spans upstream exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas, as well as downstream refining and fuel sales. By operating across the value chain, Chevron has a natural hedge that helps it weather major fluctuations in crude oil prices and fuel and other refined products.

In the third quarter, production dropped by roughly 106,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, or roughly 2.6%. This was driven in part by fewer physical barrels under production -- sharing contract entitlements and by disruptions in the Middle East. While production fell, upstream earnings surged 72% to $5.7 billion.

On top of this, downstream refining margins exploded as global refining capacity took a hit amid the Iran conflict, with strikes hitting facilities in the Middle East and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries taking roughly 10% of the world's fuel-making capacity offline. As a result, Chevron's refineries operated at 98% capacity, and downstream earnings surged 333% year over year to $4.9 billion.

Chevron is a top integrated oil and gas company vital to the energy complex, and this year illustrated the strengths of its integrated business model and capital discipline, showing why it continues to deliver for long-term investors with 39 consecutive years of dividend increases.

#3006. How To Build Financial AI Capacity As A Competitive Advantage

Dr. Ravi Gedela, CEO, Banking Labs Inc., an AI-powered financial intelligence company.

The global financial system stands at the threshold of a fundamental structural realignment driven by artificial intelligence (AI). It is a paradigm shift at its macro scale, intensified by the fast-paced penetration into vertical domains of global finance and, notably, capital markets, regulatory compliance and financial crime risk management.​

For leaders across large banks, institutional investment firms and payment service providers, navigating this shift is no longer a discretionary IT modernization effort. It is an existential imperative for long-term business growth and market leadership.

However, critical questions remain: Is AI a hyperscale trap of cash flow or a real business growth opportunity? Why do many AI programs stall in large institutions? And what must change for them to succeed?

Over the next decade, financial institutions will experience a dramatic reallocation of enterprise value. Historically, much of a firm’s value has resided in human capital: the knowledge, execution capability and client networks of senior bankers and deal teams. In the emerging operational model, that value anchor migrates to proprietary software architectures, governed data assets and institutional context layers that the firm owns.

Achieving this transition requires leadership to systematically extract the latent domain expertise, tactical judgment and deal-making frameworks locked within the minds of their top human performers and permanently embed them into software assets. By transforming ephemeral human capability into compounding firm-wide intelligence infrastructure, institutions can ensure that their competitive moat expands continuously rather than walking out the door at the close of every business day.

​A common reason AI programs stall is that they often rely exclusively on generalist frontier model providers to run complex financial operations. Frontier labs produce exceptional raw cognitive engines, but they often optimize for horizontal, mass-market scale. Treasury, capital markets and financial crime risk management, by contrast, are specialized, confidential domains governed by strict regulatory mandates, distinct data topologies and exacting precision standards.

Generalist providers are unlikely to build the last-mile intelligence pipelines that finance requires: transaction venues that comply with jurisdiction-specific rules, material non-public information (MNPI) isolation barriers and deep integrations with systems of record, such as Bloomberg or Salesforce. That work would distract from hyperscale revenue targets and add regulatory exposure.

Sustainable value, therefore, requires purpose-built financial AI: architectures that wrap foundation models in operational harnesses, compliance guardrails and domain-specific integration layers. At Banking Labs, where my team builds financial AI across capital markets, compliance and financial crime, we have consistently found that this harness, not the model itself, is where durable advantage is won.

In private markets—where workflows historically suffered from manual human coordination, fragmented data and non-standardized documentation—vertical AI architectures can systematically execute core operational processes:

1. Data Room Preparation And Tearing: Agents can autonomously ingest, organize, cross-examine and extract key metrics from incoming virtual data room documents, cross-referencing company performance against firm-specific investment mandates.

2. Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) Drafting: The system can synthesize internal financial models, market positioning data and competitive landscapes into comprehensive, publication-ready deal decks and investment committee memos.

3. Buyer Outreach And DDQ Processing: AI can facilitate the autonomous coordination of targeted buyer lists, tailored outreach tracking and the automated intake, resolution and verification of complex due diligence questionnaires (DDQs).

4. Executive Markup Workflows: These systems can help modernize senior leadership interfaces by enabling executives to mark up presentations directly on mobile devices or via email. The AI harness can parse these handwritten or text markups, execute structural edits across underlying files and return fully revised presentation decks within, in my experience, 20 minutes (down from a standard two-day turnaround using junior staff). Simultaneously, the engine can generate complete, transparent audit trails detailing every modification for junior bankers to inspect and verify.

While private markets require the constant navigation of unstructured data, public markets can present structured, data-rich environments ideal for advanced multiagent architectures. In these venues, firms can deploy sophisticated agentic frameworks, such as multiagent debate clusters. While automated execution can dramatically accelerate transaction velocity, operating at scale requires rigorous compliance architectures to ensure speed never compromises legal defensibility.​

Model risk management is being reshaped in both the United States and Canada. In April 2026, U.S. banking regulators replaced SR 11-7, the guidance that had governed model risk for 15 years, with SR 26-2. The new framework is more principles-based, and regulators have indicated that AI-specific expectations will follow.

Canada is moving in the same direction. OSFI’s revised Guideline E-23, effective May 1, 2027, brings AI and machine learning models explicitly within its scope. Its approach is proportional: Models with greater autonomy or customer impact require closer review and monitoring.

Institutions operating in both countries must therefore satisfy two regimes on different timelines. Both, however, require AI that is governed, explainable and auditable. General-purpose models struggle to meet this standard on their own. Vertical financial AI, designed with lineage and controls from the outset, is better positioned to do so.

In institutional compliance, lineage auditability outranks raw statistical accuracy. A highly accurate model that operates as a black box cannot withstand a regulatory examination or judicial discovery. In the agentic era, explaining a single model is not enough; institutions must be able to prove, step-by-step, how every AI-assisted decision was made.

This answers the questions I began with. AI can become a cash trap when institutions treat it as a technology function delegated to large vendors offering frontier models. It becomes a growth engine when they invest in domain-specific, vertical AI capacity that they own and govern. Large institutions should pivot from the convenience of outsourcing AI to the discipline of building AI capital.

Before the next budget cycle, executives should ask one question: If a regulator asked tomorrow why our AI made a specific decision, could we show them, step-by-step, how it came to that decision?​​

#3004. History Says the Nasdaq Will Soar Once Again in 2027 After the Sell-Off. The Best Growth Stock to Buy Before That Happens

Seagate's impressive growth and attractive valuation could send it on a bull run over the next three years.

Technology stocks have been crushed lately, which explains why the tech-laden Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -1.46%) index has slid by more than 5% since the beginning of October.

The meltdown in tech stocks can be attributed to several factors. From the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike in September to the likelihood of further rate hikes to control inflation to the outcome of the midterm elections, investors have become risk-averse. They are booking profits in tech stocks following a strong run over the past year and a half.

However, what's worth noting is that this isn't the first time the Nasdaq Composite index has witnessed such volatility.

The tariffs announced by President Donald Trump last year crushed tech stocks. Investors panicked amid fears that the proposed tariffs would hurt demand for chips, components, smartphones, and other things. As a result, the Nasdaq Composite slid 10% between February and April 2025. In fact, the index was down over 20% at one point in early April 2025, compared with the beginning of February.

However, the artificial intelligence (AI) gravy train shielded tech companies from any potential slowdown. This explains why the Nasdaq Composite has rallied by an impressive 44% over the past year and a half despite the recent setback. I won't be surprised to see history repeat itself, as AI's productivity gains and healthy investments in this space will ensure robust earnings growth for tech companies.

For instance, a survey conducted by the consulting giant McKinsey earlier this year found that 80% of respondents who use AI at work reported higher productivity. Meanwhile, 50% of the respondents admitted that AI is improving their decision-making capability. As a result, the adoption of AI and AI agents in enterprises is growing.

This is great news for Seagate Technology (STX -5.56%), which is benefiting big time from AI adoption and has seen a substantial slide in its stock price lately.

The past three months have been brutal for Seagate stock investors. It has lost 31% of its value over this period. However, the company is capitalizing on the deployment of AI data centers.

Seagate manufactures data storage solutions, including hard-disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), and high-capacity storage solutions for enterprises and data centers. The company's storage solutions have been supporting the global AI boom, helping hyperscalers and AI labs store massive data sets for training AI models and running inference applications.

Not surprisingly, Seagate has been enjoying stunning growth. The company's revenue in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 2) jumped 61% year over year to $4.23 billion. Meanwhile, the strong demand and short supply of HDDs sent Seagate's non-GAAP operating margin to 50.7% in the previous quarter, up from 29% in the year-ago period. The company's earnings per share (EPS) nearly tripled year over year to $7.68.

The data center business accounted for 81% of the top line, up 63% from the year-ago period. Seagate is confident of maintaining its impressive momentum. The company will finalize the configuration and pricing for its 2028 storage devices over the next few quarters, noting that the pricing environment continues to improve.

What's more, Seagate management noted on the latest earnings call that it expects further expansion in revenue and margins this year, driven "by an extremely strong demand environment with visibility extending beyond 2030." The company's guidance reflects management's claim.

Seagate expects $4.8 billion in revenue in the current quarter, implying a 70% jump over last year. Even better, its EPS is poised to nearly triple once again to $9.20. Given that Seagate sees strong demand visibility through the end of the decade, it is easy to see why analysts are projecting healthy EPS growth over the next three years.

STX EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Specifically, Seagate's earnings are predicted to jump by 157% this year, and I won't be surprised to see it outperform expectations over the next couple of years. Moreover, Seagate trades at just 14.6 times forward earnings, a discount to the tech-laden Nasdaq-100 index's forward earnings multiple of 20. Assuming Seagate trades in line with the Nasdaq's forward earnings multiple after three years and its EPS jumps to $87.28, its stock price will skyrocket to $1,745.

That's just over 3x where this AI stock is trading right now. So, buying Seagate right now could be a profitable move, especially given that a potential rally in the Nasdaq Composite next year could lift the stock out of its rut and send it on a bull run.

#3003. Top Wall Street analysts find these 3 stocks attractive as long-term investments

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

Anmuth ranks No. 832 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of about 9.40%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

#3001. Bitdeer: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Bitdeer's 3.1 gigawatts of power can earn Bitcoin mining income today while sites await long-term data center leases.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Bitdeer (BTDR -9.25%) announced an 89% year-over-year revenue increase to $320.7 million as it transitions power assets into high-performance computing data centers. The company is pivoting from volatile Bitcoin mining to long-term contracted artificial intelligence (AI) cloud infrastructure. Three things management said stand out.

Bitdeer is securing multiyear contracts for its high-performance computing (HPC, data centers built for intensive AI tasks) infrastructure and cloud services, giving the business visible cash flows that don't depend on cryptocurrency price swings.

Management is backing data center construction with asset-level debt and customer prepayments that cover more than 50% of graphics processing unit (GPU) costs, keeping share dilution low.

With 3.1 gigawatts of total power capacity, Bitdeer monetizes available electricity through Bitcoin mining while preparing sites for long-term data center leases.

Demand for artificial intelligence compute outpaces the available power supply, and Bitdeer relies on pre-energized sites, low-cost power, and proprietary hardware to convert mining locations into data centers, while maintaining financing execution and capital discipline.

The company aims to maximize returns by deploying power where economic value is highest, balancing short-term crypto earnings with long-term data center revenue.

#2993. Nvidia vs. AMD: Which Is the Better Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock for 2027 After the Tech Sell-Off?

Investors have an easy choice to make if they are looking to buy one of these two semiconductor stocks right now.

Artificial intelligence (AI) chip stocks have witnessed a brutal sell-off lately, as evidenced by the 20% dip in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index over the past month.

Not surprisingly, semiconductor stalwarts Nvidia (NVDA -13.63%) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +1.92%) have also been under pressure. While AMD has retreated 15% over the past month, Nvidia has dropped 26%, relinquishing its status as the world's largest company in the process.

However, the solid financial performance of both these companies doesn't justify their recent slide. Both Nvidia and AMD have been clocking robust growth, and they are poised to continue their momentum into the New Year. That's why I will take a closer look at the prospects and valuations of both companies to determine which one is the better semiconductor stock to buy for 2027.

Nvidia remains the dominant player in AI chips despite intensifying competition. Semiconductor supply chain data provider Silicon Analysts estimates that Nvidia will control 75% of the AI chip market by the end of 2026.

The company has been pulling the right strings to maintain its status as the top AI chip player. It is now designing server systems aimed at enhancing inference performance while reducing costs simultaneously. Nvidia claims that its latest Vera Rubin chip systems consume twice as much power as the previous-generation Blackwell processors but deliver 10x higher performance-per-watt.

Nvidia has begun shipping its Vera Rubin systems in volume to customers. It expects the platform to account for 20% of its data center revenue in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. The company should see a significant ramp in Vera Rubin sales in 2027, which will be a tailwind for its revenue and earnings growth, given the significantly higher revenue it expects from its latest systems.

It is worth noting that Nvidia has already guided for a 70% increase in its fiscal 2028 revenue (which will end in January 2028 and coincide with the majority of calendar 2027). Analysts are forecasting a 71% increase in Nvidia's earnings per share (EPS) in fiscal 2028, following an impressive 95% jump that's projected for the current fiscal year.

So, there is a solid chance of Nvidia stock stepping on the gas once again in the New Year.

Silicon Analysts notes that AMD controlled 6%-8% of the AI chip market last year. However, the company's latest quarterly results indicate that it is gaining ground in this market. AMD's data center revenue surged 97% year over year in Q3 to $8.5 billion, driven by the growing adoption of its server processors, graphics cards, and rack-scale systems.

For some perspective, Nvidia's data center revenue surged by 106% year over year in the last reported quarter to $96.2 billion. So, while Nvidia remains the significantly larger player in this segment, AMD's accelerating growth rate suggests that it is gradually catching up. Importantly, AMD expects its data center growth to accelerate.

The Q4 revenue guidance of $17 billion implies a year-over-year jump of 66%, higher than the 45% growth it reported in Q2. The data center business produced 64% of AMD's revenue last quarter, and it expects the segment to account for more than 80% of its top line in 2027. Also, AMD expects total revenue to increase by more than 80% next year, an acceleration over the 50% top-line growth it is expected to deliver in 2026.

What's more, AMD's EPS growth rate is projected to accelerate from 93% this year to 108% in 2027, according to Yahoo! Finance consensus estimates. Given that the data center segment will account for the majority of AMD's top line next year, it is evident that the company will gain more share in AI chips. So, is AMD a better AI semiconductor stock to buy compared to Nvidia?

We have seen that both Nvidia and AMD are on track to deliver impressive earnings growth in 2027. However, AMD's EPS growth is poised to be higher than Nvidia's, suggesting that it may be the better growth stock to buy.

But the valuation tilts the balance in Nvidia's favor, as evident from the following chart.

Nvidia is significantly cheaper than AMD, suggesting it may have greater upside potential once the market rewards it with a premium valuation. This is probably why Nvidia's median 12-month price target of $318 implies a potential jump of 88%, higher than AMD's projected 12-month gains of 26%.

So, Nvidia looks like an ideal investment for investors seeking a chip stock trading at attractive levels. However, they won't go wrong with AMD either, as its accelerating growth will help it justify the valuation and send the stock higher in 2027 and beyond.

#2990. History Says Investors Who Make This 1 Move During Bear Markets Always Win Out

It sounds counterintuitive, but doing nothing might be the best thing you can do.

When stock prices are falling, investors usually react in one of two ways. They decide to move to cash and wait for things to get "better," or they consider buying the dips. The problem is that both strategies require you to make a prediction, and predictions are often wrong.

Investors can't predict the future, so there's really no sense in even trying it. Staying the course regardless of what the market's doing in the short term is usually the best thing to do. That includes keeping your automatic investments right on schedule.

Unfortunately, many investors react emotionally to market developments. They see their investments declining in value, and their instinct is to stop the bleeding before it gets worse. The problem is that nobody knows exactly the right time to get in or out.

Investors usually sell only after losses have already occurred, and then buy back in only after the rebound is well underway. In either case, it usually ends up damaging long-term returns.

Buying the dip can seem wise in practice, but it still carries risks because it requires you to pick an entry point. If you overthink it, you might wait too long or not long enough. Either way, it requires you to decide what the best time is to trade.

The best idea, as it turns out, might be to do nothing at all.

Whether it's into a workplace retirement plan, such as a 401(k), or just a regular brokerage account, maintaining your automatic investment schedule is the best way to take advantage of volatile markets.

It requires no timing, no market watching, and really no action whatsoever. Continuing to invest at regular intervals allows you to buy the dips whenever they occur or accumulate long-term wealth when stock prices are near highs. Fixed contributions help lower your overall cost basis and improve your overall returns.

Some of the best options for this strategy are the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.73%) or the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.27%). But really, any diversified equity or fixed-income fund is ideal for this. The key to success is avoiding the temptation to time the market and pick your entry and exit points. By focusing on long-term wealth accumulation instead of short-term market machinations, you have a much greater chance of riding out and even taking advantage of bear markets when they arrive.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 835%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 208% for the S&P 500.

They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor.

#2986. Digi International (DGII) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue climbed 24% in fiscal 2026 as the company eyes a pending deal.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Digi International Inc. (DGII -18.80%) reported record results for fiscal 2026, highlighted by growth across all primary financial metrics and the announcement of a pending $130 million acquisition of Disruptive Technologies. Management indicated that the company is on track to reach its long-term goal of $200 million in annualized recurring revenue in fiscal 2027, one year ahead of the original 2028 target. The strategic focus remains on integrating hardware with subscription-based management services and leveraging the new acquisition to expand the SmartSense solution into European markets. Management noted that the current supply chain environment requires longer-term demand planning and surgical pricing adjustments at the individual SKU level to manage rising component costs, particularly in memory.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Fiscal Q4 2026 Digi International Inc. Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Jamie Loch, Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead.

James Loch: Thank you. Good day, everyone. It's great to talk to you again, and thanks for joining us today to discuss the earnings results of Digi International. Joining me on today's call is Ron Konezny, our President and CEO. We issued our earnings release after the market closed today. You may obtain a copy of the press release through the Financial Releases section of our Investor Relations website at digi.com. This afternoon, Ron will provide a comment on our performance, and then we'll take your questions. Some of the statements that we make during this call are considered forward-looking and are subject to significant risks and uncertainties.

These statements reflect our expectations about future operating and financial performance and speak only as of today's date. We undertake no obligation to update publicly or revise these forward-looking statements. While we believe the expectations reflected in our forward-looking statements are reasonable, we give no assurance such expectations will be met or that any of our forward-looking statements will prove to be correct. For additional information, please refer to the forward-looking statements section in our earnings release today and the Risk Factors section of our most recent Form 10-K and subsequent reports on file with the SEC. Finally, certain of the financial information disclosed on this call includes non-GAAP measures.

The information required to be disclosed about these measures, including reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures are included in the earnings release. The earnings release is also furnished as an exhibit to Form 8-K that can be accessed through the SEC Filings sections of our Investor Relations website. Now I'll turn the call over to Ron.

Ronald Konezny: Thank you, Jamie. And again, welcome, everyone, to Digi's Fourth Fiscal Quarter and Full Year 2026 Earnings Call. First and foremost, Happy Veterans Day to everyone. My father had 2 tours with the U.S. Army. So it's a very personal holiday for me. And I want to thank all those veterans for giving our country the greatest honor service to our nation. That said, we've got a good agenda for you today. We're going to review fiscal 2026 highlights. We're going to talk about some results and our guidance and give an update on our long-term goals. Some key messages for the year. As you recall, we are a customer-driven organization. Customers are our #1 priority.

We provide them a complete, secure, reliable solution for business and mission-critical applications. We devote about 15% of our revenue to innovation. Innovation spans across hardware, connectivity, software and now increasingly the use and leverage of AI for ROI. We complement this award-winning technology with impeccable service. Our customers need 24/7 expert support. They need flexible solutions, whether they self-manage them or offer Digi to fully manage those solutions. We back that up with a company that's strong, that's thriving, that's executing on its financial and operational priorities. We're happy to announce yet another set of record quarterly revenue, ARR and adjusted EBITDA metrics. And we've delivered results that are above our guidance almost across the Board.

Our ARR, which is the biggest sign of customers accepting Digi solutions is ahead of our target. We combine that financial performance, deploy organic initiatives -- with that cash we generate, we're able to finance acquisitions with debt, pay down the debt through the synergies we are able to capture. For example, recently, we integrated Jolt and Particle into common systems and processes, achieved our financial objectives. We now are on the [ precipice ] of our most recent acquisition, Disruptive Technologies, which extends SmartSense to Europe and [ CSS ] into new markets with new award-winning sensors. So the idea of acquiring, integrating, generating and compounding has now been established within Digi.

The key pillars of our IoT value proposition are a combination of security. And in today's world, security is a rapidly evolving and frequently changing landscape. The advent of AI has brought threats that are now happening on a much more frequent basis, and we are responding with zero trust device authentication and then encryption, automated vulnerability management and having certification to the highest standards of carrier-grade type security. We combine that with 4 decades of reliability, high uptime, longevity of devices that carry you through an average of a 7-year deployment, which is what many of our customers see and really redundant and fault tolerance systems.

Our offering scale both in numbers and across geographies, many of our customers need us to perform across the world. We're managing millions of edge devices. We're cloud native. We're an API-first architecture. Our solutions work as well for small businesses as they do the largest companies in the world. And they've got to be easy to use. They got it easy to provision, intuitive to use and get you really the quickest time to value with plug-and-play hardware and again, complemented by expert support.

And now with the advent of AI, we've got a fifth pillar, which is really leveraging AI, both at the edge and in the cloud to make our systems even more valuable and improving that time to value. We also offer our customers a range of models. As I mentioned earlier, customers can pursue a more traditional model where they purchase our equipment, they use our device management tools, and they really self-manage their solution. They're also increasingly a fully managed solution, where we're offering the complete solution, hardware, software, connectivity services, zero down monthly fee. And quite frankly, for many of our customers, that better matches the ROI.

They don't have a spike of ROI that then tempers over time. They actually build up overall ROI over time, and that better matches a fully managed solutions for many of our customers. In some cases, the customer never owns the equipment and what we're delivering is outcomes. That outcome may be asset uptime. It may be enhanced security, it may be leveraging field resources more efficiently. But they can really leverage the decades of our experience and excellence and decide how much effort they want to put into their IoT solution. We've had success across multiple verticals. We've been a long supplier to infrastructure, utilities and energy.

We're providing connectivity for the smart grid for meters and for renewable solutions where our routers and gateways and [ road ] manager solutions are very popular. We're very, very involved in the healthcare industry, both with medical devices through our Particle by Digi division, but also with SmartSense. We're providing temperature monitoring for sensitive medical applications. In our Opengear division, we provide out-of-band management for both data centers and edge solutions across the globe. We're also involved in retail and point of sale where we're providing really drop-in networking for the use of our digi routers and managed services.

Transportation, we are frequently deployed in a number of mass transit solutions where Digi TX routers are used for visibility of fleet telematics and enabling ridership WiFi, digital signage and other solutions. And lastly, we participate in a number of industrial manufacturing opportunities where our Particle by Digi XBee and ConnectCore solutions provide secure reliability, connectivity for remote access. As I mentioned earlier, we've developed a flywheel over my soon-to-be 12-year tenure. We are using a global database of solutions to source and eventually identify acquisitions that we think can be accretive to the value proposition for our customers and, of course, to our operational model.

We acquired those companies using debt that protects the Digi shareholder and making sure that we're building value that will accrue to the stock price, not just market capitalization. We then integrate those companies, and we take pride in integrating them into our systems, into our culture, into our processes. We then leverage growth opportunities through cross-selling, and we also then look at when appropriate cost base synergies on cost of goods and manufacturing and implement our quality initiatives. We then generate strong cash. That ARR-focused solutions provider really generates cash with a capital-light model that we can then use to repay that debt, lever down and allow us the opportunity to pursue additional acquisitions.

Our recent acquisitions of Jolt and Particle were in the last 2 years. We now have Disruptive Technology that's pending. On Disruptive Technologies, we are joining forces with a company that has, we think, the world's leading IoT sensor. As you can see here, smaller than the postage stamp, incredible versatility in the types of things it can measure and its battery life, which is up to 15 years, ease of deployment and driving ROI in some of the most unexpected places. We are purchasing Disruptive Technologies for $130 million of cash, which we're going to be funding from our credit facility. We expect it to generate $9 million in incremental adjusted EBITDA in our fiscal 2028 period.

It is subject to regulatory approval, which we expect to receive this month. And our forward guidance includes assuming Disruptive Technologies joins Digi on November 30. In calendar '25, you can see Disruptive Technologies had more of a onetime financial model where they sold sensors and had a lower subscription fee. They've deployed over 250,000 sensors. Majority of those are in Europe and many times through channel partners. Digi's model is to flip this on its edge and that recurring revenue will be the focus, and we're going to be embedding those sensors into a subscription rather than having them sold separately onetime. We think that's in the customer's best interest.

It closely matches their outcomes and, of course, helps us build ARR. Why did we choose Disruptive Technologies? As I mentioned, best-in-class sensing. Small sensors, 15-year battery life, a unique protocol, we think is industry-leading and allows us to gain an edge. It also has additional sensing capabilities that we don't offer today or we offer to third parties. We enter the European market. We are taking SmartSense on the road. We're going to leverage the relationships and channel partners that Disruptive Technologies have in place across over 20 European companies. We enter new markets of building automation, occupancy and further extending SmartSense food and healthcare markets.

As I mentioned, we're going to be transitioning DT to a subscription model, and it's going to provide even more data that establishes really the foundation for leveraging AI. We're really putting live data generators out there in the physical world. As I mentioned earlier, it will be financially accretive to Digi, especially in 2028 fiscal period where we have gone through most of our integration and are able to then accelerate its growth. I'm going to pass over to Jamie for some comments on our results and our fiscal '27 guidance.

James Loch: Everyone, nice to see you. What a great year, a milestone year for Digi. It's -- I'm in the fortunate position to be able to share the output that comes with all the things that Ron had previously talked about. So for Q4, we just had a banner year, record quarterly revenue, record ARR, record adjusted EBITDA. Our revenue growth was pretty evenly split this quarter. About $16 million of that revenue growth came from onetime revenue with about $13 million coming from recurring revenue.

Our operating leverage, which is also a really great thing to see, our operating expenses fell in Q4 to 47% of revenue, which is down year-over-year from 51% -- gross margins are down a little bit this quarter. But as we've talked about, we are in the range of the low to mid-60s, which is really the right range for us to play in. That revenue mix is going to be a partial driver from ARR growing faster than revenue. But inside then of that onetime revenue, there is product mix that will kind of get us inside of that range, and we're firmly comfortable in that range right now.

As we look deeper into our results into our segments, you can see we have strong performance against -- inside of both of our segments. Our IoT Products and Services business is up nearly 30% in revenue year-over-year with a 320 basis point improvement in operating margin year-over-year and a 100% increase in our ARR. That ARR increase is impacted by our acquisition of Particle, but there is also a nice organic growth that is taking place inside of that number. In our Solutions business, our 20% revenue growth, with a nearly 600 basis point improvement in our operating margin year-over-year and an 11% increase in our ARR number.

And you can see that ARR number is right on the edge of 200, which we'll talk about here in a minute. That wraps up then for the year and what an absolutely incredible year it was for Digi. Record revenue, record ARR, record adjusted EBITDA. You can see nearly 25%, 24% to be exact on revenue growth. That revenue growth is really split about 50-50 between onetime and recurring. Strong operating margins, strong GAAP EPS, continued growth in our adjusted EBITDA and our adjusted EBITDA margins. Our operating leverage fell for the year from [ 48% ] to 49% from 50% for the full year.

Gross margins, while down a little bit in Q4 on the heels of what was very strong margin performance for the year was up year-over-year on fiscal '26. So just an absolute record year, a phenomenal performance by all of our teams. That's great to see it manifested in the P&L. It's a good sign that customers are getting the services and the support that they need to hit their critical objectives. Ron talked about the flywheel. And one of the things that Digi is very proud of is kind of old school fundamentals. We generate profits and we generate cash. In this quarter, we generated $42 million in cash.

That puts us over our adjusted EBITDA number for the year, $153 million of cash for the year. That leads to a debt balance of gross at $69 million. But really from a net debt perspective, when you look at the cash on hand, we're right at $39 million, well below even a onetime lever. So at this point, it's just phenomenal to see the flywheel fully into effect. It puts us in a position to execute on disruptive and follow the same pattern where we will generate cash and move that debt down. Moving into our guidance for fiscal '27. We are right now projecting that our ARR growth for fiscal '27 will be at least 15%.

For the year, we're anticipating revenue growth to be between 10% and 15%. We're anticipating our profit growth to be between 12.5% and 17.5%. This guidance, as Ron indicated, does include Disruptive Technologies. That was announced on October 1. We are anticipating a close date of November 30. And as a reminder, Particle closed in January of 2026. You can see on the chart on the left where it kind of lands from a midpoint perspective with those ranges in terms of dollars. Very excited to see continued double-digit growth throughout all 3 areas of our main P&L lines.

Specifically for Q1, we are anticipating revenue growth to be between 14% and 18%, adjusted EBITDA growth to be between 25% and 30% and our adjusted net income per diluted share to have growth of 27% to 34%, which is an assumption on 39.5 million shares. Again, the guidance includes Disruptive Technologies closing on November 30. Reminder that particle closed in January. That -- the adjusted net income number per diluted share does include interest expense, which we anticipate to be between $0.02 and $0.04 per diluted share for FQ1. We mentioned this briefly on our main 5-year goals.

We had indicated at the end of 2023 that we wanted to have $200 million in ARR and $200 million in adjusted EBITDA by the end of '28. You can see that based on our guide, we would expect to be able to deliver on that ARR objective here in '27, which is a year early. You can see on the adjusted EBITDA at the midpoint, right, we've got a little bit of work to do. It is a 15% CAGR through from the time we set the goal through '26. And so we fully anticipate that we will meet this objective by the end of '28 as we originally outlined. But just absolutely phenomenal performance.

It's great to see us continuing to execute on the objectives that we've laid out and continue to deliver on the commitments that we've made. So with that, we will take your questions. And so operator, please provide our participants instructions to ask a question.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question comes from Tommy Moll of Stephens.

Thomas Moll: I wanted to start with the demand update. What can you tell us about the opportunity pipeline? And I know the days to win KPI is one that's helpful. So please give us an update there.

Ronald Konezny: Let me start with the funnel, the pipeline. It's up double digit. It's actually the highest it's ever been. I'm going to have Jamie comment on some of our progression of those opportunities, but we're seeing great deal registration, great channel participation and our direct selling business units within solutions are also seeing really record pipelines.

James Loch: Yes, Tommy, I think on the days to win, it continues to improve. I think there was maybe a little bit of a slowdown in that improvement. I think the elections bring or brought at least a level of uncertainty and maybe a little bit of wait and see. But they continue to improve, which is a good sign. I would say they are not back to pre-COVID levels, but they are improving sequentially, and they continue to improve year-over-year. So we continue to see that moving in the right direction.

Thomas Moll: And then I wanted to ask about the recurring revenue guide, 15% for the year. Even if I strip out Disruptive, I think it would still imply maybe like a 13% growth rate. So solidly double digit and pretty healthy. What gives you the confidence that you can execute at that level in the coming 4 quarters?

James Loch: Yes. Tommy, great question. I think some of the data we shared on the pipeline and being predictive about how those opportunities are going to progress throughout the sales stages and ultimately win rates, that's giving us a lot of confidence that we've got a good handle, especially over the external factors. But we've got enough, I think, history experience. We've got brand-new products. I think we're leading in IoT AI deployment, both at the edge and at the cloud. And I think customers with the risk that's being increased almost daily with security and support, customers are increasingly saying, "You know what, I can't do this internally anymore.

I need help." I need to manage my IoT assets as actively and carefully as I do my IT assets. And I think that goes right into Digi's value proposition.

Operator: And our next question comes from Scott Searle of ROTH Capital Partners.

Scott Searle: Nice job on the quarter, nice to also see continued strong growth into fiscal '28. Maybe to start on the supply chain and gross margins, a little bit challenged this quarter, but still well within the targeted range. I wonder if you could just talk us through some of the puts and takes in terms of what you're seeing out there. There's a lot of talk not just about memory, but certainly extended lead times and other components. How you guys are managing that and how that's kind of crafting your outlook for gross margins over the next couple of quarters?

James Loch: Yes. Scott, you mentioned it's a difficult environment out there. The AI data center surge and build-out has really put a lot of pressure on the supply chain, especially memory. But it's spilled over into other components as well that are fighting for capacity all the way down to the fab level. I can't give our team enough credit in collaboration between the demand side of our equation within our business units and of course, our supply chain professionals. They are out there taking advantage of decades-long relationships with both first and second-tier type of providers in coordination with a global set of contract manufacturers. We have both cost challenges and allocation challenges.

We're fighting through those allocation challenges pretty well. The cost challenges, quite frankly, are unavoidable. We're being very, very thoughtful and surgical down to the SKU level of when we can use price to help capture some increased costs and quite frankly, where we can't. And we're always being mindful of that solution revenue to make sure we're not putting our ARR at risk. We're playing a long game with our customers. We don't want to take advantage of any kind of onetime or transitionary increase in pricing. We do think eventually memory pricing will stabilize. None of us know exactly when, but I think I'm really proud of the team for fighting through it.

Scott Searle: Great. And if I could follow up on Opengear and out-of-band management. I'm just wondering if you could give us some thoughts in terms of what you're seeing overall demand, kind of the growth expectations there, particularly when you look at some of the opportunities for you, whether it's in Neocloud or hyperscalers, which you guys have not historically participated. How should we be thinking about that opportunity as we enter fiscal '28?

James Loch: Yes. The Opengear team is a great team with a great leader. They're having really broad-based growth. And what I mean by that is both campus and edge deployments in addition to data center opportunities. They're growing as strongly in Europe and APAC and LatAm as they are in the U.S. I mean they've really become a bit of a global standard within smart out-of-band console server. And we're excited to try to continue that success by landing potentially a hyperscaler. That's a long road, and we're very well along that road. There are no guarantees, but we're fighting hard.

In many cases, we do business with them, but not in their core cloud business, but with their IT groups or with maybe smaller offerings that're not as large and central as their core data center application. But we're really excited about some of the progress we're making.

Operator: And our next question comes from Matthew Maus of B. Riley Securities.

Matthew Maus: Congrats on the strong close to the fiscal year. Just to quickly go over ARR again. In terms of Disruptive, I'm wondering how quickly do you expect disruptive customers to move to the SmartSense subscription model and how you think that shapes ARR for fiscal '27 and beyond?

James Loch: Yes, it's a great question. We haven't quite closed the transaction yet. So a lot of this execution is yet to remain. There's a lot of course planning discussions happening between the teams right now. We're going to be very deliberate and careful, and '27 will be a year of transition. If you recall, a lot of disruptive technologies relationships are through channel partners. So there's a combination of working directly with end users, but also working closely with the channel partners, both in Europe and in the U.S. So we do think it will take some time to transition. We're patient. We're long-term thinkers.

We're going to be very deliberate and thoughtful, but we do think that transition will happen over time. But it will be a very thoughtful, gradual. It won't be a snap the chalk type of transition.

Matthew Maus: Got it. Sounds good. It was also great seeing a strong outlook for fiscal '27. I pretty sure the slides mentioned it includes Disruptive. So I'm just wondering how we should think about the organic growth embedded in that 10% to 15% range and what would get you toward the upper end?

James Loch: Yes. It's Disruptive Technologies that we just talked about. It's going to be a little different than what they've experienced historically, where historically, they would see very, very strong growth rates on the onetime ARR, not maybe as strong because the revenue model was much more onetime oriented. So you're going to see really a shift from that onetime growth into recurring. Recurring will then much more closely match the Digi model where recurring revenue grows faster than that onetime.

Matthew Maus: Got it. And last one for me, just in terms of -- for the future, like which end markets are you most excited about for the near term? Is it data centers, utilities, healthcare or some other?

James Loch: I'm sorry, Matthew, I think we lost you a little bit in the audio. I believe you might be asking about where we're seeing pockets of strength in verticals.

Matthew Maus: Yes. So in terms of end markets, I'm wondering like what you're most excited about for the near term? Is it data centers, utilities, healthcare or some other?

James Loch: Yes. We touched on it earlier in the presentation. And those verticals we touched on, and you can see how diverse our business is and our different product lines have different strengths. So in healthcare, SmartSense and our Particle by Digi had great success in utilities. We have great success in cellular routers. Thank you, Jamie. We do a lot of work with our Ventus by Digi solution in financial services and point of sale. So you've got -- these are the verticals we are most excited about that we think are really powering our growth, both in the past and we think into the future.

Matthew Maus: Great. That was all for me. Congrats on the strong quarter. I'll hop back into queue. Thank you.

Operator: And our next question comes from Timothy Shubsda of Piper Sandler.

Timothy Daniel Shubsda: This is Tim on for Fish here. Just wondering if you could kind of talk about how you guys are feeling about supply versus the level of demand that you've been seeing in terms of like your 2027, how are your supply levels in terms of like your guidance? Are you kind of on track? Or do you have ample supply? Do you still need to go out and get some more?

James Loch: Yes. Timothy, it's a really good question. We generally are in the mode where demand is not as big a challenge as supply is. And as I mentioned, we've got just a great collaboration between our product lines, understanding their demand, educating their customers on lead times. And of course, our supply chain group really resourcefully finding all of the components we need, not always at the price we'd like, but nonetheless, fighting through this. We also are having to look farther out than we have traditionally. A lot of times, we're looking out 6 months on our demand planning. Now we're having to go to 9 months, in some cases, as far as 12 months.

And it is a really careful message that we manage with our customers. Of course, we've got SKUs that are high runners, and we're using a lot of our historical demand numbers to help guide. But then there are some other SKUs that are more unique to certain applications or customers. And those -- we have to have really collaborative discussions with our customers that are seeing either increases in their business or having to offer a new market or new offering. And we're having to get them to commit earlier to make sure we've got the product to meet their time lines.

Timothy Daniel Shubsda: Got it. And you guys have mentioned kind of security here kind of being a little bit of a motivating factor for customers. In terms of just general customer behavior, have you guys been seeing like more of a pull in, any pushouts or anything to comment on there?

James Loch: Yes, we don't see any dramatic pulling in or pushing out. Our price increases when they do go in effect for certain SKUs have been pretty modest, single-digit type of situation. So not enough to really dramatically change behavior. I'd say lead times has probably been a bigger opportunity for us to work through to make sure people are thinking 3, 6, in some cases, 9 months out on their demand side, recognizing that some of these solutions may be harder to procure, take more time. But we're not seeing significant pull in or push out. We still think customers are really ROI driven.

And in some cases, our best prospect is the customer has been managing their own IoT solution internally and have realized, boy, it is no longer set and forget it. You have to really actively manage these solutions. You have to have security staff that are monitoring [ CVEs ], putting patches and solutions in place and then able to get those solutions out to these edge devices be it an automated software platform in addition to protecting your cloud and API assets. So I think this day of managing internally is becoming more and more burdensome for those companies that have chosen that path.

Operator: And we have a follow-up from Tommy Moll of Stephens. Your line is open.

Thomas Moll: Just a question on the first quarter guidance, Jamie. EBITDA dollars are guided down sequentially. What can you highlight as the driver there?

James Loch: Yes, Tommy, I think maybe a couple of things. One, based on a lot of what Ron has talked about relative to the supply chain, I think we're maybe guiding a little bit more of the margins to be in the middle of our kind of range as opposed to on the higher end. And so I think we'd probably see them maybe being down a little bit. I think as you walk into the first quarter, there are certain expenses that occur in the first quarter that don't occur at the tail end of the year due to some seasonality that takes place. And so it's that combination that maybe has you a tick down on a sequential basis.

Ronald Konezny: And seasonally, for our IoT Products and Services segment, where they really all their work through channels, a lot of channel partners really like to tighten up their inventory positions prior to their fiscal year-end. So [indiscernible], have been the slower start for our year.

Thomas Moll: Great. Thanks for the insight. That's all I needed.

Operator: And we have a follow-up from Scott Searle of ROTH Capital Partners.

Scott Searle: Ron, 2 quick follow-ups. First, on Disruptive, given the battery life and the overall RF performance of the solution, I'm wondering if you're thinking about as driving it as something more broad. For instance, cellular and WiFi are standards-based solutions, but we've also had nonstandards-based solutions that became de facto places in the marketplace, things like LoRa. And so I'm wondering if you're thinking about this more broadly or too early to contemplate on that front.

James Loch: Well, it's a good question, Scott. I think our first stage in thinking about this is actually internally beyond SmartSense. So we're going to get the solution in the hands of our cellular business unit, our Opengear business unit, our Particle business unit, so they can better understand the technology and look for applications. So for example, we service a lot of financial institutions. We provide connectivity to their ATMs. Disruptive Technology has a door open, door closed solution. Very, very potentially great feature for our ATM customers to know when that safe has been accessed, right, and coordinating that with their field services resources. There's a lot of those applications we think we can lock in a data center.

A lot of these conditions need to be monitored, temperature, water, may be in some's cases. So we think there's some great opportunities there to monitor our customers' IT assets and the environment that surrounds them. So we think that first step is really leveraging it internally. There certainly is the potential to take our show on the road, especially with the particle group that takes this type of technology puts it in a package like an XP or a ConnectCore and then allows others to incorporate this technology into their devices. That's going to be a little bit further out. Embedded solutions take time. But I think we've got a lot of opportunities internally beyond SmartSense.

Scott Searle: Got you. Very helpful. And if I could, as I look out at the landscape, what you guys do very well in addition to connectivity is reliability and security thrown on top of that and you're bringing edge processing to the equation. So with that stated, markets that come to mind are things like defense tech, drones, robotics, which we haven't heard you guys talk a lot about. So I'm wondering if you could kind of frame the opportunity for you in those verticals? Or do they just not have enough interest given, I'll call it, the other nuances that go along with them?

James Loch: No, it's a very good point you bring up, Scott. And you've seen some other companies that have had success in defense, AeroTech. That's not traditionally an area that we've had a lot of exposure to. And we're seeing that if you can get a snowball going in those verticals, they can develop into a reliable source of customer satisfaction and, of course, revenues for us. So we do a little bit of work in that area, not quite as much as we'd like. We talk a lot about devoting resources specifically to high-growth applications, and those are certainly a few of them that come to mind.

Operator: I'm showing no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn it back to Ron Konezny for closing remarks.

Ronald Konezny: Thank you. And I want to thank everybody for joining the call today during the results of what's really been a breakthrough fiscal 2026 for Digi. I want to thank, first and foremost, our team. This is a team sport. I can't be prouder of our leadership team, the entire company, collaborating both on their business units and functional areas, but also as we survey the market, both Digi and non-Digi customers. We always come out top on reliability, quality, service and support, and that's a testament to the team. I want to thank our suppliers as well. Without them, we can't build these great solutions that our customers enjoy.

We're going to be at the Stephens [ Growth ] Conference next week in Nashville. So please, if you get time, say hi to us, and we'll be able to share more of our story at that event. So I want to thank everybody for joining the call, and we're looking forward to our next update.

#2985. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Dodge ranks No. 476 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.5%. See Brookfield Infrastructure Partners KPIs on TipRanks.
